questions.title: What is an API, REST endpoint and SDK?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: An API is a contract for interaction; an endpoint exposes an operation; an SDK packages convenient client-side code.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: RESTful designs use resources and HTTP semantics where appropriate. An SDK wraps transport, schemas, authentication hooks and errors, but the server still owns business rules and authorization. Version both client and server contracts.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A Python SDK method calls a Java status endpoint and converts the response into a typed object.

followups.question: Is FastAPI an SDK?
followups.answer: No. It is a web framework for building APIs; you can separately build an SDK that calls those APIs.

followups.question: What is OpenAPI?
followups.answer: A machine-readable API description useful for documentation and client generation; generated clients still need semantic tests.

questions.title: What do HTTP status codes 400, 401, 403, 404, 429 and 5xx mean?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: They communicate different classes of request, identity, access, availability and server failure.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: 400 usually signals an invalid request; 401 missing/invalid authentication; 403 denied access; 404 missing resource or deliberate concealment; 429 rate limiting. 5xx indicates server-side failure, but retry safety depends on the operation. Keep internal details out of public error messages.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A 429 may include Retry-After, while an invalid account format should be corrected rather than retried.

followups.question: Should every 5xx be retried?
followups.answer: No. Use idempotency and a bounded policy; a timeout or server error can occur after a write committed.

followups.question: Why not always return 200 with an error string?
followups.answer: It confuses clients, monitoring and retry behavior. Use a consistent status and structured error contract.

questions.title: What is connection pooling?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Reuse a bounded set of expensive connections rather than opening a new one for every operation.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Size pools across all replicas against the database/service capacity. Configure acquisition timeouts and release connections reliably. A pool improves reuse but cannot make a slow database infinitely parallel. Long transactions can exhaust it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Ten API replicas with pools of 20 can attempt 200 connections, not just 20 globally.

followups.question: Why can more connections hurt?
followups.answer: They can increase database contention and memory use while worsening queueing.

followups.question: How do you detect a leak?
followups.answer: Track acquired/idle connections, wait time and request completion; inspect paths that fail to close or return connections.

questions.title: What is rate limiting versus concurrency limiting?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Rate limiting controls work per time interval; concurrency limiting controls simultaneous work.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: A provider may cap requests/minute, tokens/minute and active calls independently. Use bounded queues, per-tenant fairness and distributed coordination when limits apply across replicas. An in-process semaphore only controls one process.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Five replicas each allowing 20 calls can create 100 calls against a provider whose total limit is 20.

followups.question: What is a token bucket?
followups.answer: A budget refills over time and permits bursts up to its capacity. Choose the unit, such as requests or estimated tokens, to match the constrained resource.

followups.question: What happens when the queue fills?
followups.answer: Reject or defer work with a clear busy response and retry guidance; do not let memory grow without bound.

questions.title: What is CORS, CSRF and XSS?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: CORS governs browser cross-origin access; CSRF abuses authenticated browser requests; XSS injects executable content into a page.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Use server-side authorization regardless of CORS. Cookie-based authentication needs appropriate CSRF protections and cookie settings. Escape/sanitize rendered content, especially model output and retrieved documents, and avoid unsafe HTML insertion.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A chatbot displaying raw HTML from a model could execute an injected script if the UI trusts it.

followups.question: Does JSON prevent XSS?
followups.answer: Only if it is rendered safely as data; inserting a JSON string into HTML unsafely can still be exploitable.

followups.question: Is hiding an API key in frontend code safe?
followups.answer: No. Browser code and bundles are visible to users; privileged secrets belong on a protected server.

topics.title: GPU & vLLM
topics.description: Memory arithmetic, batching, kernels, quantization and serving diagnosis

intro.label: Architecture
intro.text: API admission and token budget -> bounded request queue -> tokenizer -> inference scheduler -> prefill -> iterative decode with KV cache -> detokenization and streaming. Observe queue time, token lengths, active sequences, memory and request outcomes together.

questions.title: Why use a GPU, and when is inference compute-bound or memory-bound?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: GPUs perform many operations in parallel. Inference can be limited either by arithmetic throughput or by moving model data through memory.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Large matrix operations can exploit GPU parallelism, but achievable performance depends on batch shape, precision, kernels and memory bandwidth. Prefill often has high arithmetic intensity; small-batch autoregressive decoding often spends heavily on reading weights and KV state. These are workload tendencies, not guarantees. CPU work, tokenization and network delays can also dominate.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If a short-output service has low GPU utilization but long queue times, inspect batching and CPU bottlenecks before buying more GPUs. If decoding bandwidth is saturated, simply increasing clock or theoretical FLOPS may not help much.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: GPU utilization, memory bandwidth, kernel timing, queue time, TTFT, TPOT and completed output tokens/second.

followups.question: Why does peak TFLOPS not predict application tokens/second?
followups.answer: Peak values assume particular precisions and ideal kernels. Real serving includes memory movement, communication, variable sequences, scheduling and non-GPU work.

followups.question: Can CPU inference be appropriate?
followups.answer: Yes, for small models, low request rates or latency-insensitive tasks when its measured cost and latency fit. GPU deployment is not automatically economical at low utilization.

questions.title: Prefill versus decode: what happens in each phase?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Prefill processes the prompt. Decode generates the answer one token step at a time for each sequence.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Prefill computes representations and key/value states for prompt tokens. Decode reuses cached keys/values and computes the next position, avoiding recomputation of the full prefix. The cache grows with sequence length. Prompt length primarily affects prefill work and stored state; output length adds sequential decoding steps. Batching changes the efficiency of both phases.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A 12,000-token document with a 20-token answer stresses prefill differently from a 100-token prompt with a 2,000-token answer. Benchmark both rather than reporting one generic latency number.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Optimizing long-prompt throughput can hurt short-request latency if scheduling does not provide fairness.

followups.question: Does KV caching make long-context decoding free?
followups.answer: No. New tokens still attend to prior state in ordinary attention models, and the cache occupies memory. Accessing a long cache can increase decode cost.

followups.question: What is chunked prefill?
followups.answer: The scheduler processes long prompts in portions so they can coexist more fairly with other work. It can improve responsiveness under mixed workloads, with configuration-dependent throughput trade-offs.

questions.title: Estimate model-weight memory before deployment.

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Multiply the number of parameters by bytes per stored parameter, then reserve additional memory for runtime needs.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: A 7-billion-parameter model at two bytes/parameter needs about 14 GB decimal for weights alone. Four-bit storage has a theoretical payload of 3.5 GB, but scales, zero points, unquantized layers, alignment and runtime workspaces add overhead. Serving also needs KV cache, activations, kernels and allocator headroom. Training adds gradients and optimizer state.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A model whose weights nearly fill a 16 GB device may load but fail when requests allocate KV cache. Fit should be evaluated at the required concurrency and sequence lengths, not only at startup.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Peak allocated and reserved device memory, cache occupancy, OOM frequency and usable concurrency under the intended workload.

followups.question: Is BF16 smaller than FP16?
followups.answer: Both commonly use 16 bits per value. They differ in exponent and mantissa allocation, affecting range and precision, not basic storage size.

followups.question: Can I infer memory from the model name?
followups.answer: Not reliably. Check actual parameter count, architecture, quantization format, expert structure and loaded tensors. Some layers may remain higher precision.

questions.title: Derive KV-cache memory and explain GQA/MQA.

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: The cache stores a key and a value for each retained token in each attention layer. More tokens and active sequences require more cache memory.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: For a conventional decoder estimate bytes = 2 * layers * KV_heads * head_dimension * bytes_per_element * retained_tokens, summed across sequences. The factor 2 is keys plus values. Grouped-query attention uses fewer KV heads than query heads; multi-query attention commonly shares a single KV head. Cache layout, sliding windows, quantization and distributed placement can change actual allocation.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128 and FP16 cache, each token needs 131,072 bytes, or 128 KiB. A single 8,192-token sequence uses about 1 GiB of KV payload. Sixteen such sequences need about 16 GiB before paging overhead and weights. These are hypothetical dimensions, not a claim about your deployed model.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Smaller KV precision or fewer KV heads can reduce memory, but architecture and supported kernels constrain choices and quality must be validated.

followups.question: Should I use total attention heads in this formula?
followups.answer: Use KV heads, which can differ from query heads under GQA/MQA. Check the checkpoint configuration.

followups.question: Does four-bit weight quantization also make the KV cache four-bit?
followups.answer: Not automatically. Weight and cache precision are separate configuration and kernel-support decisions.

questions.title: What are vLLM and PagedAttention?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: vLLM is an LLM serving engine. PagedAttention organizes KV memory in blocks so variable-length requests can use memory more efficiently.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Logical sequence blocks map to physical cache blocks rather than requiring one large contiguous allocation per sequence. This reduces waste from over-reservation and fragmentation and supports efficient scheduling. It does not compress model weights or remove the mathematical need for token state. Its benefit depends on request lengths, sharing, scheduling and hardware.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: When one request finishes, its blocks can be reused for another request. This is more flexible than reserving each request's maximum context capacity from the start.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Cache utilization, concurrent token capacity, throughput at a latency SLO and OOM/preemption behavior.

followups.question: Is PagedAttention the same as an operating-system swap file?
followups.answer: No. The analogy is block-based address management; it is not a claim that GPU cache is automatically swapped to disk.

followups.question: Does it guarantee faster single-request latency?
followups.answer: No. Its key advantages are memory management and serving efficiency. Measure latency and throughput under the intended concurrency rather than assuming every request gets faster.

questions.title: Static batching, dynamic batching and continuous batching: compare.

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Static batching fixes a group of requests. Dynamic batching collects nearby arrivals. Continuous batching can change the active group as decoding proceeds.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Fixed batches waste capacity when short sequences finish before long ones. Continuous scheduling admits new work into freed capacity between decoding iterations, subject to token and memory budgets. Fairness, long prefills and variable output lengths still need management. Larger batches can improve throughput while worsening queueing or per-token latency.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A batch with answers of 10, 20 and 1,000 tokens wastes resources if it waits as a rigid group. A continuous scheduler can replace completed sequences with new requests.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Aggressive utilization can reduce interactive responsiveness. Separate latency-sensitive and batch workloads when their requirements conflict.

followups.question: Why not set maximum batch size as high as possible?
followups.answer: Memory, latency and scheduling overhead impose limits. Optimize throughput subject to TTFT/TPOT and error constraints, not the batch-size number itself.

followups.question: What is token-based admission?
followups.answer: Capacity is budgeted using prompt and expected/generated token work rather than treating every request as equal. It better captures the difference between tiny and long-context requests.

questions.title: Prefix caching, semantic caching and response caching: how do they differ?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Prefix caching reuses model computation for an identical token prefix. Response caching reuses a finished answer. Semantic caching reuses results for sufficiently equivalent queries.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: KV-prefix reuse can reduce repeated prefill work but does not eliminate generation of new output tokens. Correct reuse depends on matching model, tokenizer, adapter and relevant execution configuration. Application response caches additionally need corpus and permission/version validity. Tenant separation and potential side channels require deliberate design.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Many requests share a long stable system prompt. Prefix reuse may help. If the user-specific text appears first, fewer prefix tokens may be reusable. Reordering text only for caching must not break semantics or access controls.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Prefix hit rate, saved prefill tokens/time, TTFT improvement and isolation-test results.

followups.question: Can prefix caching answer a new question without decoding?
followups.answer: No. It reuses prefix computation; the new answer still requires inference.

followups.question: Can cached KV state bypass authorization?
followups.answer: Authorization must happen before protected content is included, and caches must be scoped appropriately. Cached computation is not permission to expose source data.

questions.title: Tensor, pipeline, data and expert parallelism: when do you use them?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Tensor parallelism splits layer computation; pipeline parallelism splits layers; data parallelism runs replicas; expert parallelism distributes experts in suitable models.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Tensor-parallel workers exchange intermediate results and benefit from fast interconnects. Pipeline stages pass activations and can have bubbles or imbalance. Independent serving replicas can scale throughput when the model fits each replica. Expert routing adds communication and load-balancing considerations. Choose topology from model fit, workload and measured communication overhead.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If a model fits on one device and traffic grows, replicas may be simpler than splitting it across devices. If it cannot fit, model parallelism becomes necessary, but a slower network can limit scaling.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Scaling efficiency, interconnect utilization, per-stage idle time, throughput and tail latency.

followups.question: Does two GPUs always mean twice the throughput?
followups.answer: No. Communication, scheduling, imbalance and bottlenecks can make scaling sublinear or even harmful for small workloads.

followups.question: Is training data parallelism identical to serving replicas?
followups.answer: No. Training typically synchronizes gradients; serving replicas can handle independent requests without gradient synchronization. Use precise terminology.

questions.title: Quantization, FlashAttention, TensorRT and speculative decoding: what do they optimize?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: These target different costs: numeric storage/compute, attention memory traffic, compiled execution and the number of serial generation steps.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Quantization reduces numerical precision with format- and kernel-dependent quality/performance effects. FlashAttention reorganizes exact attention computation to reduce memory traffic; it is distinct from KV-cache paging. TensorRT/TensorRT-LLM provide optimization and execution capabilities whose support depends on model and hardware. Speculative decoding proposes tokens with a draft mechanism and verifies them; correct algorithms preserve the target distribution under their assumptions.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A draft model that rarely agrees with the target can add overhead rather than speed up generation. Measure acceptance rate and net latency. A quantized model may save memory but lose accuracy on numeric extraction.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Faster kernels and lower precision improve only the bottlenecks they target. Pin compatible versions and rerun quality tests after optimization.

followups.question: Does FlashAttention make attention linear-time?
followups.answer: Ordinary full attention still has quadratic pairwise work; the optimization primarily changes memory access and intermediate storage. Do not confuse it with architectures that alter attention complexity.

followups.question: Can I claim TensorRT and vLLM are one identical stack?
followups.answer: No. State which engine and kernels were actually used, for which model and benchmark. Do not combine tool names into an unsupported implementation claim.

questions.title: Requests hit OOM or p95 rises sharply. What do you investigate?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Look at active tokens and queueing before assuming the model itself suddenly became slower.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Compare prompt/output distributions, concurrent sequences, KV occupancy, preemption, memory fragmentation and model copies. Check whether web workers each loaded an engine. Inspect CPU tokenization, network/provider latency and scheduler limits. Apply admission control, context/output caps, batching changes or additional capacity based on the identified cause.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A new feature sends full chat history on every turn. Prompt lengths grow, KV memory increases and prefill delays interactive requests. Summarize or retrieve relevant history with provenance and validate that important constraints are retained.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: TTFT/TPOT percentiles, completed RPS, token throughput, OOM rate, queue age and cost per accepted answer.

followups.question: Is reducing context length always safe?
followups.answer: No. It can remove evidence or user constraints. Measure quality on long-context tasks and reject oversized requests explicitly rather than silently truncating critical data.

followups.question: How do you benchmark a fix?
followups.answer: Replay a representative sanitized workload with fixed versions, warm-up, offered load and timing boundaries. Include failed and cancelled requests, not only successful fast ones.

questions.title: How should you defend DGX Spark and GPU optimization on your resume?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Describe the exact machine, model, engine and experiment you used. Hardware branding alone is not evidence of optimization.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: DGX Spark uses NVIDIA GB10 and a unified-memory design; do not describe it as a conventional discrete GPU with independently usable advertised VRAM. Verify OS/architecture, driver, framework, model and precision compatibility. A vendor maximum-model claim is a capacity statement under assumptions, not your measured serving throughput.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Prepare an experiment ledger: checkpoint/revision, quantization, context limit, batch/token budget, engine/version, warm-up, workload, before/after latency and peak memory. Leave unknown values as evidence to collect rather than inventing them for the interview.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Record reproducible baseline and optimized results; no throughput or speedup is asserted here for your hardware.

followups.question: What if I used a hosted NVIDIA endpoint instead?
followups.answer: Say that clearly. Calling an endpoint is different from operating or optimizing a local GPU server. The current SQL Copilot provider report does not contain a completed NVIDIA benchmark.

followups.question: What is the strongest optimization story?
followups.answer: One where profiling identified a bottleneck, a targeted change improved a measured metric, quality stayed within a defined bound and you can explain the new trade-off.

questions.title: What are CUDA, ROCm and a GPU kernel?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: CUDA and ROCm are GPU computing software ecosystems; a kernel is a function executed on a device.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Compatibility depends on hardware, drivers, runtime, framework build and the specific kernels needed by a model. CUDA and ROCm are not interchangeable labels. A framework may hide low-level calls, but deployment still depends on the supported stack.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A quantization method supported on one NVIDIA device may lack an efficient implementation on a different platform.

followups.question: Does having a GPU guarantee acceleration?
followups.answer: No. The operation must run on supported device kernels with enough parallel work to outweigh overhead.

followups.question: What should you record in a benchmark?
followups.answer: Device, driver/runtime, framework/engine version, model revision, precision, sequence lengths and workload.

questions.title: What are FP32, FP16, BF16, INT8 and INT4?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: They are numerical representations with different precision, range and storage costs.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: FP32 uses 32 bits, FP16/BF16 16 bits, and integer quantization can store values in fewer bits with scales/other metadata. BF16 has a wider exponent range than FP16 but fewer fraction bits. Quantization schemes and kernel support determine actual speed and error.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A four-bit weight format reduces nominal payload but may leave activations and KV cache in higher precision.

followups.question: Is smaller precision always faster?
followups.answer: No. Dequantization and unsupported kernels can offset memory savings. Benchmark the complete workload.

followups.question: Why test numeric tasks after quantization?
followups.answer: Small representation changes can affect rare tokens, numbers and reasoning behavior differently from average text quality.

questions.title: What is VRAM, unified memory and memory bandwidth?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Memory capacity is how much fits; bandwidth is how fast data can be moved. Unified-memory designs have a different sharing model from conventional separate CPU/GPU memory.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Capacity constraints and bandwidth constraints are distinct. A model can fit but decode slowly. Host/device transfers and shared-memory contention can dominate. Use the actual hardware architecture and runtime measurements rather than equating all advertised memory with dedicated GPU VRAM.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: DGX Spark requires discussing its unified-memory design; the same capacity number does not imply identical performance to another accelerator.

followups.question: Why can a smaller model still be slow?
followups.answer: Low batch utilization, transfer overhead, CPU preprocessing or inefficient kernels may dominate.

questions.title: What is a warm-up run, and how do you benchmark inference fairly?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Warm-up lets initialization and compilation settle before measuring steady-state serving, while cold-start performance is measured separately.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Pin inputs, versions, output policy and concurrency. Report cold and warm behavior, successful and failed requests, prompt/output length distributions and timing boundaries. Compare engines under equivalent quality and sampling assumptions.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Run a representative replay after loading the model, then separately measure startup and first-request latency.

followups.question: Can I time only GPU kernels?
followups.answer: That helps diagnose compute but excludes tokenization, queues and network delivery. User-facing performance needs end-to-end timing too.

followups.question: Why are averages insufficient?
followups.answer: Tail latency, overload and failures can be hidden. Report percentiles, offered/achieved load and errors.

topics.title: SQL Copilot
topics.description: Planner-first design, safe querying, joins, semantics and database operations

intro.label: Architecture
intro.text: Natural-language question -> intent/entities -> authorized schema retrieval -> semantic definitions -> relationship graph and join candidates -> explicit query plan -> SQL generation -> dialect-aware AST/schema/policy validation -> coverage and calibrated confidence -> clarification or controlled execution boundary -> result checks and explanation. Execution is a design stage here; verify its actual deployment in your project before claiming it.

questions.title: Why planner-first Text-to-SQL instead of sending the whole schema to an LLM?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Make the meaning, tables and relationships explicit before producing SQL. This makes errors easier to detect and explain.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Retrieve relevant schema and business definitions, resolve entities, identify grain and measures, discover joins, then construct a plan with filters, aggregation and output requirements. A deterministic planner can constrain generation and expose missing information. Whole-schema prompting can work for small schemas, but becomes expensive and distracts the model as schema size and ambiguity grow.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 'Top customers by revenue last quarter' requires a revenue definition, time zone, date field, refund treatment and ranking grain before selecting tables. SQL can be syntactically valid while answering the wrong business question.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Plan correctness, schema/column recall, join correctness, clarification quality and final semantic success.

followups.question: Why not use only templates?
followups.answer: Templates are reliable for a narrow known query set but may not cover ad hoc combinations. A hybrid can route common tasks to templates and use constrained planning for broader cases.

followups.question: What does a plan contain?
followups.answer: Required entities, measures, dimensions, filters, join keys, cardinalities, aggregation grain, ordering/limit and unresolved assumptions. Keep it structured and inspectable.

questions.title: How do schema linking and business vocabulary resolution work?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Translate business language into authorized tables and columns without inventing missing fields.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Index table/column descriptions, aliases, data types, relationships and approved metric definitions. Combine exact lexical matches with embeddings when useful. Sample values can help entity resolution but may contain sensitive data; expose only permitted summaries or controlled lookups. Separate schema evidence from generic SQL examples.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 'Active client' may map to customer_status='ACTIVE', but only if the business definition says so. 'Revenue' may require net amounts after refunds rather than summing a column named amount.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Rich metadata improves linking but needs governance and freshness. Incorrect descriptions can systematically mislead the planner.

followups.question: What if two columns both seem plausible?
followups.answer: Ask a targeted clarification or use an authoritative semantic definition. A confidence score should not conceal unresolved ambiguity.

followups.question: Can Spider examples provide a missing enterprise column?
followups.answer: No. Generic examples can illustrate SQL patterns but cannot establish your private schema or business semantics. If a required attribute is absent, clarify or reject the unsupported request.

questions.title: How do you discover multi-table joins, and why is shortest path not enough?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Use known relationships to connect required tables, but choose joins according to business meaning and row cardinality.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Represent tables as nodes and validated relationships as edges with key columns, direction/cardinality and optional semantic labels. Search candidate connecting paths, then check whether they preserve the desired grain. The shortest graph path may use an irrelevant relationship or multiply rows. Inferred joins from similar column names require validation.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Joining orders to order_items and payments can multiply each payment by each line item. Aggregate each one-to-many relation to order grain first or use a correct alternative plan before combining them.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Required-table recall, unnecessary-table rate, edge/path correctness, cardinality violations and execution-equivalent results.

followups.question: How do bridge tables affect planning?
followups.answer: Many-to-many relationships often require a bridge and can change counting semantics. Decide whether to count rows, distinct entities or weighted allocations.

followups.question: Why is table recall not enough?
followups.answer: You can retrieve every correct table and still choose wrong keys, omit filters or aggregate at the wrong grain. Evaluate joins and outputs separately.

questions.title: How do you validate SQL safely beyond checking for SELECT?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Parse SQL, restrict what it can access and execute, and enforce limits in the database as well as the application.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Use a dialect-aware AST parser, require the intended single-statement form, allowlist accessible objects/functions and reject unsupported constructs. SELECT can still invoke dangerous functions, leak forbidden rows or run an expensive query. Use a least-privilege read-only account, row/column controls, timeouts, resource limits and result-size caps. Parameterize user values rather than concatenating strings.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A SELECT from a sensitive payroll table is unacceptable for a user without permission even though it does not modify data. A Cartesian join over huge tables can exhaust resources without any write operation.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Strict allowlists reduce risk but limit expressiveness. Expose unsupported queries clearly instead of weakening controls silently.

followups.question: Why not regex alone?
followups.answer: SQL syntax includes nesting, comments, quoting and dialect-specific constructs. Regex checks are brittle; parsing plus database enforcement provides stronger boundaries.

followups.question: Does AST validity prove correctness?
followups.answer: No. It checks structure and selected policies. Business meaning and result correctness require semantic validation or evaluation against expected outcomes.

questions.title: How do retries and confidence gates improve Text-to-SQL?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Use a specific error to repair a query, and stop when the problem requires clarification rather than another guess.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Feed constrained validator feedback into a bounded repair process. Distinguish syntax errors, unknown columns, missing requirements, ambiguous semantics and permission failures. Permission failures must not trigger attempts to bypass policy. Confidence should combine evaluated signals and be calibrated; a self-assigned score or deterministic heuristic is not a probability until validated.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If the query omits a requested date filter, regenerate with that explicit requirement. If 'current exposure' has two business definitions, ask the user instead of repeatedly sampling SQL.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Repair success by error type, average attempts, semantic drift, false acceptance and p95 end-to-end latency.

followups.question: Can retries inflate success while harming latency?
followups.answer: Yes. Report first-attempt success, eventual success, attempts and latency/cost together. Additional retries may produce diminishing returns.

followups.question: What if the corrected SQL changes the question?
followups.answer: Re-run coverage against the original request and preserve user-approved constraints. A valid but simplified query should not be labeled a successful repair.

questions.title: Explain SQL validity, execution accuracy and test-suite accuracy.

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: SQL validity asks whether a query passes defined checks. Execution accuracy asks whether its result matches the expected result. Neither should be confused with a generic success score.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Define validity precisely: parser validity, schema validity and policy validity are different. Result comparison needs handling for ordering, duplicates, nulls, numeric tolerance and nondeterministic functions. One database instance can make different queries accidentally produce the same result; multiple carefully chosen test databases can expose semantic differences. A benchmark's success field must be traced to its scoring code.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: SELECT COUNT(*) and SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) may match on a dataset with one row per customer, but differ when duplicates are introduced. Passing one execution result is weak evidence of general equivalence.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Execution evaluation is more realistic but requires safe datasets and careful expected-result design.

followups.question: What is wrong with comparing SQL strings only?
followups.answer: Equivalent queries can use different aliases or join formulations. Structural comparison and execution-based tests are more informative, though each has limitations.

followups.question: What should I say about my 120-case report?
followups.answer: It records 67.5% success, 78.33% validity, 79.17% join success and 93.15% average table recall. Establish the report's scoring definitions; do not rename its success as proven live-database execution accuracy.

questions.title: INNER versus LEFT JOIN, WHERE versus HAVING, and COUNT variants?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: INNER JOIN keeps matches; LEFT JOIN preserves left rows even without a match. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups. COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) ignores nulls.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: SQL uses three-valued logic for nulls. A WHERE predicate on a nullable right-side column after a LEFT JOIN can remove unmatched rows and effectively change the intended outer-join behavior. COUNT(DISTINCT column) removes duplicate non-null values. Define the business grain before choosing a counting expression.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: To include customers with no orders, LEFT JOIN orders and place a qualifying order-status predicate in the join condition if unmatched customers must remain. Filtering that status in WHERE usually removes them.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Validate edge cases with no matches, nulls, duplicate keys and multiple child rows.

followups.question: Why does NULL = NULL not behave like ordinary equality?
followups.answer: NULL represents unknown/missing, so the comparison is unknown rather than true. Use IS NULL for null tests and understand dialect-specific null-safe comparisons.

followups.question: Can HAVING replace every WHERE condition?
followups.answer: It may be inefficient or change meaning because filtering occurs after grouping. Apply row filters before aggregation when that matches the task.

questions.title: How do window functions differ from GROUP BY?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: GROUP BY collapses rows into groups. Window functions calculate across related rows while retaining row-level output.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: A window specifies partitioning, ordering and optionally a frame. ROW_NUMBER gives a unique sequence under a defined order; RANK and DENSE_RANK handle ties differently. Running totals depend on frame semantics; an implicit default can differ from the intended row-by-row calculation. Add deterministic tie-breakers when stable results matter.

blocks.label: Code
Example
blocks.text: Use an outer query or CTE filtering rn=1 to get the most recent order per customer. The secondary order_id makes equal-date ordering deterministic under the chosen rule.

followups.question: Why not MAX(order_date) alone?
followups.answer: It gives a date per group, not automatically the entire corresponding row, and ties may produce several rows when joined back.

followups.question: What is a CTE?
followups.answer: A named query expression that improves structure and can support recursion in supported dialects. Do not assume it is always materialized or always faster; inspect the optimizer plan.

questions.title: How do indexes and EXPLAIN help a slow query?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: An index can reduce the data scanned for selected access patterns. EXPLAIN shows how the database plans to execute a query.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Inspect estimated rows, access paths, join order, sorts and temporary work; compare estimates with observed execution where safe. Composite index usefulness depends on predicate/order structure and the engine. Indexes consume storage and slow writes. Non-sargable expressions, implicit casts and stale statistics can prevent good access plans.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A query filtering tenant_id and created_at may benefit from a matching composite index, but the choice depends on selectivity and workload. Avoid adding an index merely because a column appears in a WHERE clause.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Rows examined, execution time, buffer/cache behavior, lock waits, write overhead and plan stability.

followups.question: Why can an index be ignored?
followups.answer: A scan may be cheaper for a large fraction of the table; statistics, expression shape or ordering requirements may also matter. The optimizer's decision must be assessed with real cardinalities.

followups.question: Should an LLM create indexes automatically?
followups.answer: It can propose candidates, but resource impact, write overhead and production rollout require controlled review and testing. An assistant should not receive unrestricted DDL rights.

questions.title: Transactions, isolation, backups and DBA support: what must you know?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Transactions group changes reliably; isolation governs concurrent visibility; backups are useful only if restoration works.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Explain atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability without implying isolation always means serial execution. Know common anomalies such as dirty/nonrepeatable reads and phantoms, with engine-specific behavior. Investigate locks and deadlocks using database tools, keep transactions short and retry selected deadlock failures safely. Separate replication for availability from backups for recovery.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: DBA support may mean query troubleshooting, permissions, health checks and assisting restore tests. Do not claim ownership of cluster design or recovery objectives unless you actually had that responsibility.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Backup/restore success, replication lag, slow-query rate, lock waits, recovery time and access-change auditability.

followups.question: RPO versus RTO?
followups.answer: RPO is the acceptable data-loss window; RTO is the target time to restore service. A backup schedule alone does not establish either without tested recovery.

followups.question: Why can a read replica return stale data?
followups.answer: Replication may be asynchronous. Route tasks requiring current state appropriately and expose freshness when necessary.

questions.title: What are primary keys, foreign keys and cardinality?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: A primary key identifies rows; a foreign key expresses a reference; cardinality describes how many rows can relate.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: One-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many relationships affect joins and aggregation. A column name ending in id is not proof of an enforced relationship. Inspect constraints and approved business semantics.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Customers to orders is often one-to-many; orders to products may use an order_items bridge.

followups.question: Can a foreign key be nullable?
followups.answer: Depending on schema rules, yes; missing relationships affect join semantics.

followups.question: Why does cardinality matter for sums?
followups.answer: Joining multiple one-to-many tables can multiply rows and double-count amounts unless the plan preserves the intended grain.

questions.title: What are normalization and denormalization?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Normalization separates data to reduce certain redundancies; denormalization deliberately combines or duplicates data for access needs.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Choose based on consistency, write patterns and analytical performance. A normalized schema can require more joins, while a denormalized model can simplify reads but needs update correctness. Do not assume either is universally faster or more correct.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A reporting table may precompute daily totals, while transactional data remains normalized.

followups.question: Should a copilot use raw tables or a semantic layer?
followups.answer: A governed semantic/reporting layer can reduce ambiguity for common metrics, but its freshness and definitions must be explicit.

followups.question: Can denormalization create stale answers?
followups.answer: Yes. Refresh lag and inconsistent updates must be measured and communicated.

questions.title: What is SQL injection and how do parameters help?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Injection occurs when untrusted input changes query structure instead of remaining a data value.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Bind values through the database driver rather than string concatenation. Identifiers such as table names often cannot be parameterized the same way, so validate them against an allowlist/schema. Generated SQL still needs AST, object and resource controls.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A customer name containing quotes must remain a parameter value, not become part of executable SQL syntax.

followups.question: Does parameterization make all generated SQL safe?
followups.answer: No. The query can still access forbidden data or be too expensive. Permissions and policy validation remain necessary.

followups.question: Why not just escape quotes?
followups.answer: Manual escaping is dialect- and context-sensitive and easy to get wrong. Use supported binding APIs.

questions.title: What are subqueries, CTEs, UNION and UNION ALL?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: They combine or structure query results in different ways.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Subqueries nest a query; CTEs name intermediate expressions; UNION combines compatible results and removes duplicates; UNION ALL preserves duplicates. Optimizer behavior and syntax vary by dialect. Choose according to intended semantics before performance.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Combining transactions from two non-overlapping partitions may use UNION ALL, while deduplication requires a deliberate key policy.

followups.question: Does a CTE guarantee caching?
followups.answer: No. Materialization/inlining depends on engine/version and query. Inspect the plan.

followups.question: Why can UNION hide a bug?
followups.answer: Removing duplicate rows can conceal an incorrect join or unexpected duplication rather than fixing its cause.

intro.label: Architecture
intro.text: Source commit -> CI checks and artifact build -> image/model registry -> staging and evaluation -> controlled rollout -> health/readiness checks -> traffic -> metrics/logs/traces -> rollback. Runtime services use scoped identities, managed secrets and durable data stores.

questions.title: How would you deploy a GenAI application on AWS?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Separate the web/API service, background ingestion, persistent data and model inference so each can scale and fail independently.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: A possible design uses a load balancer, containerized API, object storage for documents, a durable queue for ingestion, a database for metadata and a model endpoint or GPU service. Select concrete services based on requirements; EC2, container platforms and managed inference have different control/operations trade-offs. Use private networking where appropriate, scoped IAM roles and centralized observability.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An upload stores a file and enqueues a versioned job. The API serves queries without waiting for parsing. Inference capacity scales from active work/queue indicators, not simply the number of web requests.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Availability, p95 latency, queue age, cost per task, deployment failure rate and recovery time.

followups.question: Why not put everything on one server?
followups.answer: It may be fine for a small prototype. Production isolation, independent scaling and recovery requirements often justify separation. Explain the workload that makes the extra complexity worthwhile.

followups.question: Why not serverless for every component?
followups.answer: Startup, execution duration, GPU requirements and dependency sizes can make some workloads unsuitable. Managed/serverless components remain useful where their limits fit.

questions.title: What Linux checks do you perform when an application is down?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Check the process, listening port, recent logs and resource pressure, then follow the failing dependency.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Inspect service status and journal logs, process/CPU/memory usage, disk space/inodes, network listeners, DNS and connectivity. Check configuration changes, permissions, certificate expiry and dependency health. Use targeted commands and preserve incident evidence; repeated restarts can hide the cause or worsen load.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text:
# Read-only diagnostic examples; replace service and port.
systemctl status myapp --no-pager
journalctl -u myapp --since '30 minutes ago' --no-pager
ss -lntp
free -h
df -h

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The process is alive but readiness fails because database connections are exhausted. Restarting every instance simultaneously may create a reconnection storm; inspect pool sizing and slow transactions first.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Time to detect, time to mitigate, recurrence, resource saturation and customer-visible failures.

followups.question: Liveness versus readiness?
followups.answer: Liveness asks whether the process should be restarted. Readiness asks whether it should receive traffic. A dependency outage should not automatically trigger endless restarts if the process can recover.

followups.question: What if disk is full?
followups.answer: Identify the responsible filesystem and files, check log rotation and retention, and follow an approved cleanup/recovery procedure. Do not blindly delete database files or active logs.

questions.title: What makes a Bash script safe and maintainable?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Validate inputs, quote variables, check failures and make reruns predictable.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Use explicit arguments, safe temporary files, cleanup traps and clear exit codes. set -euo pipefail can catch some errors but has shell-context exceptions and is not a substitute for explicit checks. Never use eval on untrusted input. Avoid logging secrets. Use locks or idempotent operations if scheduled runs can overlap.

blocks.label: Code
blocks.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
url=${1:?Usage: healthcheck.sh URL}
if curl --fail --silent --show-error --max-time 5 "$url"; then
  printf '\nHealth check passed\n'
else
  printf 'Health check failed\n' >&2
  exit 1
fi

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A health-check script is a small unit you can explain completely. A deployment script should additionally record artifact version, validate configuration, verify readiness and support rollback.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Shell is useful for orchestration, but complex data transformations and retry state are often clearer in Python.

followups.question: Why quote "$variable"?
followups.answer: Unquoted expansion can cause word splitting and glob expansion, changing arguments unexpectedly. Quoting is especially important for paths and user-provided values.

followups.question: Does set -e guarantee every error stops execution?
followups.answer: No. Its behavior depends on constructs such as conditionals and pipelines. Handle important failures explicitly and test the script under those paths.

questions.title: How do you deploy and roll back an application on a Linux server?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Deploy a versioned artifact, verify it before receiving traffic and keep a known-good version available.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Run under a dedicated low-privilege service identity, use a service manager, externalize configuration and secrets, and configure graceful shutdown. Apply migrations using a backward-compatible expand/contract strategy when possible. A code rollback cannot undo an incompatible database migration automatically. Separate deployment success from application readiness.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Start the new release on a separate port, run health and representative functional checks, then switch the proxy or load balancer. Keep the prior artifact until rollback conditions are cleared.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Deployment duration, error-rate/latency regression, rollback time and change-failure rate.

followups.question: What if requests are in flight?
followups.answer: Drain connections and allow a bounded graceful period. Durable jobs must be resumable; do not assume killing the process safely cancels external side effects.

followups.question: Blue-green versus canary?
followups.answer: Blue-green switches between environments; canary gradually sends a subset of traffic to the new version. Both need compatibility, observability and a rollback plan.

questions.title: What should a production Docker image contain?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Only the application and required runtime dependencies, built reproducibly and run with limited privileges.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Pin appropriate dependencies and base versions, use multi-stage builds where useful, exclude secrets and local caches, and run as a non-root user when possible. Image layers are immutable, so deleting a secret in a later layer does not make its earlier inclusion safe. Keep persistent data outside the container filesystem and set resource limits.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Build the API separately from a large model artifact where that suits the deployment. Reproducible model downloads need checkpoint revisions and integrity checks, not an unpinned latest reference.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Smaller images reduce transfer and attack surface, but aggressive minimalism can complicate debugging; use controlled diagnostic tooling rather than adding secrets or compilers indiscriminately.

followups.question: Is a container a VM?
followups.answer: No. It typically shares the host kernel while isolating processes and resources. Security and compatibility assumptions differ from a full virtual machine.

followups.question: What is Docker Compose useful for?
followups.answer: Defining a reproducible local multi-service environment. It does not by itself provide every production scheduling, resilience and security capability.

questions.title: What belongs in CI/CD for a GenAI system?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Test software behavior and model-system quality before promoting a change.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Run lint/type checks where useful, unit/contract tests, security/dependency checks, image builds and a representative evaluation suite. Version prompts, datasets, retrieval configuration and model adapters as deployable artifacts. Use regression gates for critical tasks and access-control behavior. Slow comprehensive evaluations can run separately from fast pull-request checks, but promotion criteria must be explicit.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A prompt change passes code tests but reduces abstention on unsupported financial questions. The quality gate should catch it before a broad rollout.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Regression escape rate, evaluation variance, release lead time, deployment failures and rollback success.

followups.question: How do you handle nondeterministic evaluations?
followups.answer: Use stable cases, repeated measurements where justified, tolerance bands and human adjudication for consequential changes. Avoid a flaky gate based on one sampled response.

followups.question: Can I roll back only the prompt?
followups.answer: Yes if prompt/model/tool/schema versions remain compatible. Track the whole configuration bundle so a rollback restores a coherent system.

questions.title: React state, props, effects and rendering: what should you know?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Props pass data into components; state stores changing component data. Rendering describes the UI for the current inputs. Effects synchronize with systems outside rendering.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Keep state minimal and place it at the right shared owner. Use stable keys for list identity. Effects are not a general place for every derived calculation; derive values during rendering when appropriate. Handle cleanup and stale async responses so an older request does not overwrite a newer result.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A SQL Copilot page stores the current question, request status and result. If the user submits a second query, cancel or ignore the first response using a request ID rather than letting the older SQL replace the new result.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: State libraries can help complex applications, but small local state should remain simple. Your resume states basic React/Next.js knowledge, so demonstrate concrete implemented screens.

followups.question: Why not mutate state objects directly?
followups.answer: React relies on state updates and identity changes to schedule predictable rendering. Use updates that preserve the intended immutable data flow.

followups.question: Why can an effect run more than expected in development?
followups.answer: Development checks and dependency changes can expose unsafe effects. Make setup/cleanup correct rather than relying on a single invocation assumption.

questions.title: Next.js server versus client components: what belongs where?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Server components can perform server-side work; client components handle browser interactivity and browser APIs.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Keep secrets and privileged service calls on the server. A client-side component boundary affects what code and serialized data reach the browser. Rendering and caching behavior depend on the Next.js version and route configuration, so verify the project's version. Server rendering does not automatically authorize data access; every server-side fetch still needs policy checks.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Render a permitted schema summary server-side, while the query editor and streaming display run interactively in the browser. Do not embed API keys or unrestricted database credentials in client bundles.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Initial load, interaction latency, bundle size, failed requests and unauthorized-data tests.

followups.question: Is hiding a button an authorization control?
followups.answer: No. Users can call backend endpoints directly. The server must enforce the action regardless of UI state.

followups.question: Can server caching leak user data?
followups.answer: Yes if cache scope and keys ignore identity/permissions. Treat personalized responses differently from public static content and validate framework caching behavior.

questions.title: How do you design a trustworthy SQL/chatbot UI?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Show what is happening, what evidence supports the answer and whether an action has actually completed.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Distinguish planning, validation, execution and final results. Present source citations, timestamps, clarifications and explicit incomplete/error states. Avoid displaying a heuristic confidence number as guaranteed accuracy. For privileged actions, show exact parameters and impact before the required approval. Keep technical implementation details out of ordinary user flows unless they aid a decision.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A SQL preview should state that validation passed but execution has not occurred. A failed stream should not look like a completed answer with an empty final section.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Successful task completion, correction rate, abandonment, duplicate-action rate and time to resolve ambiguity.

followups.question: How do you prevent duplicate submissions?
followups.answer: Disable accidental duplicate UI actions where appropriate, but rely on server-side idempotency for real protection. Browser controls alone cannot guarantee exactly one operation.

followups.question: How do you collect feedback?
followups.answer: Attach feedback to a request/configuration ID and ask for actionable categories such as wrong source, wrong filter or missing detail. Sanitize free-text feedback and separate it from trusted instructions.

questions.title: Node.js, Python and Java: how do you compare backend choices?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Choose based on the workload, ecosystem and team's ability to operate the service, not a blanket fastest-language claim.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Node.js has an event-loop model suited to many I/O workloads, while CPU-heavy JavaScript can block that loop without worker separation. Python has a strong ML ecosystem and several concurrency models. Java/Spring Boot offers a mature enterprise ecosystem with its own threading, resource and operational choices. Network calls, database plans and model inference often dominate language overhead.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Retain a stable Java business service, provide a Python SDK for AI integration and use Next.js for the web UI. This is a defensible separation when contracts and observability are consistent.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: A polyglot system gains ecosystem fit but requires more build, deployment and debugging expertise.

followups.question: Why use microservices instead of a monolith?
followups.answer: Independent ownership/scaling can justify them, but distributed failures, deployments and data consistency add cost. A modular monolith may be simpler for a small team or tightly coupled workflow.

followups.question: What should I say about Soven Developer experience?
followups.answer: Explain one actual feature, API integration, bug and validation process. Do not inflate earlier Node.js/React exposure into ownership of systems you did not build.

questions.title: What are IAM roles, least privilege and secret management?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: IAM controls access to cloud resources; least privilege grants only needed permissions; secret management keeps credentials out of code.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Prefer workload identities and short-lived credentials where supported. Scope roles by operation/resource, rotate secrets and audit access. Application-level tenant authorization remains necessary even when cloud IAM is correct.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An ingestion worker can read its input bucket and write its index artifacts without admin access to the whole account.

followups.question: Why not use one shared admin key?
followups.answer: It increases blast radius and weakens attribution. Separate responsibilities and identities.

followups.question: Does encryption replace access control?
followups.answer: No. An authorized decrypting service can still disclose data incorrectly unless application policy is enforced.

questions.title: What are a load balancer, reverse proxy and API gateway?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: They sit in front of services to route traffic or apply shared network/API behavior.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Load balancers distribute requests across healthy instances; reverse proxies forward requests and may terminate TLS; API gateways can add authentication integration, quotas and routing. Products overlap, so describe the functions used rather than assuming every feature exists.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Multiple stateless API replicas share external state and are removed from traffic when readiness fails.

followups.question: Does a load balancer make the app stateless?
followups.answer: No. You must externalize or deliberately partition durable state; sticky sessions do not fix crash recovery.

followups.question: Where should rate limits apply?
followups.answer: At suitable global and per-tenant boundaries, with downstream-specific limits as well.

questions.title: What are horizontal scaling, vertical scaling and autoscaling?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Horizontal scaling adds instances; vertical scaling adds resources to an instance; autoscaling adjusts capacity from measured signals.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Select signals that reflect the bottleneck: queue age, active tokens or request concurrency may be more informative than CPU for LLM services. Account for startup time, cooldowns, maximum capacity and downstream limits.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Adding API replicas does not help if a single model endpoint is already saturated.

followups.question: Why can autoscaling oscillate?
followups.answer: Noisy signals and aggressive policies can repeatedly add/remove capacity. Use appropriate windows, hysteresis and minimum warm capacity.

followups.question: Can scaling solve inefficient SQL?
followups.answer: Sometimes capacity buys time, but poor plans can overwhelm any reasonable scale. Fix the bottleneck as well.

questions.title: What are availability, durability, RPO and RTO?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Availability means the service can be used; durability means stored data survives; RPO/RTO define recovery objectives.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Replication improves some failure tolerance but can replicate corruption or deletion. Backups and tested restores address different risks. Specify which data may be lost and how long recovery may take, then validate with exercises.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A vector index can be rebuilt from durable source files, but that rebuild time may exceed the desired recovery target.

followups.question: Is a backup successful if upload completed?
followups.answer: Not enough. Verify integrity and restoration under realistic conditions.

followups.question: Why distinguish index from source durability?
followups.answer: Indexes are derived artifacts; losing originals or metadata can make faithful reconstruction impossible.

questions.title: What are metrics, logs, traces and alerts in operations?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Metrics summarize trends, logs record events, traces connect a request across stages, and alerts notify on actionable conditions.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Use stable labels and correlation IDs, protect sensitive fields and define retention. An alert should identify an owner and response, not merely report every noisy fluctuation. Link high-level symptoms to detailed traces.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An alert on queue age triggers investigation of model capacity; the trace shows whether time was spent waiting or generating.

followups.question: Why not log every token and document?
followups.answer: Cost, privacy and data volume can overwhelm usefulness. Collect only what is needed and permitted.

followups.question: What is alert fatigue?
followups.answer: Too many low-value notifications train responders to ignore them. Use actionable thresholds, grouping and runbooks.

topics.title: Production scenarios
topics.description: Detailed systems questions modeled on your examples, with step-by-step answers and follow-up chains
sections: How to answer a production scenario

intro.label: Note
intro.text: These designs expand the examples you supplied. Begin with requirements and assumptions, draw the architecture, explain what each layer does, then handle the follow-ups. They are proposed designs, not assertions that every component is deployed in your SQL Copilot. The current inspected backend is Flask/ASGI; FastAPI replicas below are a hypothetical scaling option or a separate service design.

questions.title: How would you scale SQL Copilot for 100 simultaneous users?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Share stable infrastructure, isolate each user's state and bound work at every scarce dependency. One hundred users should not create one hundred uncontrolled model calls and database connections.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Browser -> gateway/auth/rate limits -> stateless API replicas -> isolated graph execution and durable state -> shared authorized schema retrieval -> global model admission queue -> LLM service -> validated read-only query service -> result/audit. Metrics and traces cover every boundary.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: First clarify whether 100 means connected users, in-flight requests or requests/second, and define input/output sizes and latency targets. Keep sessions/checkpoints outside API processes and authorize every thread lookup. Share immutable versioned schema indexes where safe; keep conversation history, retrieved private results and permissions isolated. Apply provider-wide concurrency and token/rate limits, not only a semaphore per process. Use bounded queues with deadlines and fair tenant scheduling. Database pool capacity must be budgeted across all API replicas. If execution is included, use least-privilege credentials, statement timeouts and resource caps. Long-running jobs belong in durable workers, and in-flight operations need explicit failure/retry semantics.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Suppose the provider allows 20 active calls and 100 requests arrive at once. At most 20 enter inference; the remaining 80 wait only if queue capacity and their deadlines permit. Reject or defer excess work cleanly. Do not claim all requests will finish in five seconds without a service-time distribution and load test.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: p50/p95/p99 end-to-end and stage latency, model queue age, token throughput, pool wait, timeouts, tenant fairness, cross-user isolation tests and cost per completed correct task.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: More replicas increase cost and connection demand. Caches reduce work but add freshness and isolation requirements. Longer queues absorb bursts but worsen tail latency; controlled rejection may protect existing work.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would make the API stateless, keep every user's graph state isolated and centralize limits around model and database capacity. Shared schema indexes can be reused under authorization, while conversation state cannot. I would define deadlines and bounded queues, recover durable work after crashes and validate the design with realistic load tests rather than equating replicas with capacity.

followups.question: Why multiple API instances?
followups.answer: Stateless replicas allow horizontal scaling and failure isolation. They help only if the bottleneck is at the API layer or available downstream capacity exists. External state allows any healthy replica to continue a request or conversation under authorization.

followups.question: What is Redis doing?
followups.answer: It may support caching, short-lived state and rate-limit coordination. Assign each use a durability/failure policy. Durable business records or checkpoints should use a store whose guarantees match the requirement; do not treat an optional cache as the only permanent truth.

followups.question: How do you isolate LangGraph state?
followups.answer: Use separate authenticated tenant/conversation execution IDs, validate ownership before checkpoint access and avoid a global mutable state object. An ID naming convention alone is not authorization.

followups.question: Why is a local semaphore insufficient?
followups.answer: Five processes each allowing 20 calls can send 100 calls in total. Coordinate a global limit through a gateway/shared admission service or distribute a safe quota across replicas, with failure behavior defined.

followups.question: What if SQL becomes the bottleneck?
followups.answer: Inspect pool wait, query plans, locks and execution time. Improve queries, cap expensive work and use suitable read replicas only where their lag is acceptable. More API workers can make the database problem worse.

followups.question: What if an instance crashes?
followups.answer: The load balancer stops new traffic to it. Durable work resumes from recorded state, while uncertain side effects use idempotency/status reconciliation. A retry is not proof the previous attempt had no effect.

followups.question: How do you prove it supports 1,000 users?
followups.answer: Use representative ramp, burst and sustained-load tests, recording offered versus achieved load, queueing and errors. Test long prompts and provider/database slowdowns, not only cached short requests.

questions.title: How would you ingest and index 100,000 mixed documents?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Inventory the corpus, route files to suitable parsers and process them through a restartable pipeline. Document count alone does not determine size or cost.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Source inventory -> original object storage and manifest -> durable queue -> format-specific workers -> normalization/OCR quality -> structure-aware chunks -> bounded embedding batches -> lexical/vector/metadata stores -> validation -> active-version publication.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Sample files by type, size, language and quality. Record source ID/version, checksum, permissions, bytes/pages, status and processing configuration. Preserve originals and parse PDF, Office, HTML and scans appropriately; avoid OCR when native text is reliable. Keep headings, tables, units and source coordinates. Use stable document/chunk IDs and separate stage status so retries resume safely. Batch embeddings by token/request limits, with backpressure from downstream storage. Quarantine repeatedly failing files in a DLQ with actionable errors. Validate source counts, metadata, sample extraction and retrieval quality before exposing a new index version.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For an illustrative 500 million tokens, 400-token windows and 50-token overlap imply roughly 1.43 million chunks before real boundary effects. At 1,536 float32 dimensions, raw vectors are about 8.8 GB decimal; metadata, indexes, replicas, files and headroom are additional.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Inventory reconciliation, document/page/chunk throughput, queue age, parse/OCR failures, embedding cost, freshness/deletion lag, retrieval relevance and answer quality by source type.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: More workers can overwhelm parsers, model quotas or storage. High throughput is not success if extraction loses tables or permissions. Start with a representative benchmark before scaling the full corpus.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would build an inventory and versioned manifest, preserve originals, and use asynchronous format-aware workers. Chunking and OCR would follow document structure. Stable IDs, bounded embedding batches and backpressure make retries safe. I would validate both completeness and retrieval quality before publication, and estimate capacity from sampled token counts rather than file count alone.

followups.question: Why inventory before processing?
followups.answer: It reveals unsupported formats, duplicates, oversized files, access rules and cost drivers. It also provides a reconciliation ledger so missing documents are visible.

followups.question: Why store original files separately?
followups.answer: Search indexes are derived artifacts. Originals and metadata allow reprocessing, citations, audit and recovery when an index or parser changes.

followups.question: Why not send all documents in one embedding request?
followups.answer: Provider token/payload limits, memory and failure recovery make that impractical. Use bounded batches with per-record identity and result validation.

followups.question: What if one 500-page PDF is huge?
followups.answer: Process pages/sections incrementally with resource limits and a document manifest. Preserve cross-page relationships where needed, but do not require the whole file's decoded content in memory.

followups.question: How do you handle identical files with different ACLs?
followups.answer: Share storage only with separate source references and permissions. Deduplication must not merge access rights or erase provenance.

followups.question: How do you handle an embedding worker crash?
followups.answer: Retry the same versioned job, detect completed chunk IDs and upsert missing work. Publish only when the document version meets completeness and quality checks.

followups.question: How does this differ from SQL schema ingestion?
followups.answer: SQL Copilot primarily indexes tables, columns, keys, relationships and business definitions. Keep general document knowledge separate and route questions appropriately rather than pretending every PDF is schema truth.

questions.title: A technical manual contains prose, APIs, code and tables. Which chunking do you choose?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Use a strategy matched to the content rather than one arbitrary fixed size everywhere.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Parsed blocks and headings -> content-type classification -> prose splitter / API-code units / table row groups -> parent-child links -> token-limit checks -> retrieval benchmark -> selected configuration.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Begin with structure-aware boundaries. For ordinary prose, a recursive baseline can preserve available separators; configure token counting separately. Keep API endpoint, parameters and response semantics together. Split large tables into row groups with repeated headers/units and stable identifiers. Preserve code syntax/context and parent sections for expansion. Compare a small set of chunk sizes/overlaps on representative queries while keeping other components fixed. Recursive splitting is a heuristic and still needs inspection.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Splitting 'threshold applies except to corporate accounts' after 'except' can reverse interpretation. Parent context or a larger structural unit may be necessary, even when the smaller chunk has a strong similarity score.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Evidence Recall@k, answer correctness, citation span precision, duplicate context ratio, mean/percentile chunk tokens and ingestion/query cost.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: A specialized pipeline takes more engineering but preserves meaning. A simple baseline is easier to operate and should remain the comparison point.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would preserve structure first, use recursive splitting for suitable prose and specialized handling for APIs, code and tables. I would tune sizes and overlap through a controlled evaluation, using parent expansion where small chunks lose necessary conditions.

followups.question: Why not fixed-size?
followups.answer: It is an inexpensive baseline but can break logical units. It can still win on uniform text; judge by evidence recall and answer quality rather than a universal preference.

followups.question: Why not semantic chunking?
followups.answer: It adds embedding/threshold work and can create variable sizes or poor boundaries in code/tables. Use it when measured benefits justify the cost.

followups.question: How do you choose overlap?
followups.answer: Start modestly, enforce overlap smaller than size and measure boundary recall against duplicate storage/context. Tables often need repeated headers rather than arbitrary token overlap.

followups.question: What if chunks are too small or large?
followups.answer: Small chunks lose context and increase count; large chunks dilute relevance and consume prompt budget. Parent-child retrieval can balance localization with context, but expansion must preserve permissions.

followups.question: How do you choose the winner?
followups.answer: Evaluate retrieval and end-to-end answers by document type, including exceptions, numeric tables and long sections. Report token/storage/latency cost alongside quality.
