questions.title: A reversal query retrieves settlement documents. How do you debug it?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Find the stage that lost or misranked the actual reversal procedure.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Source inspection -> parsed chunks -> query/rewrite -> lexical and dense candidate inspection -> authorized filters -> fusion/reranking -> context selection -> answer. Compare the correct source at each boundary.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Verify the source exists, is current and accessible. Inspect extracted text and chunk context before changing the model. Compare lexical and dense results independently, including exact identifiers and synonyms. Check whether a rewrite changed reversal into settlement, whether filters excluded the source, or whether reranking/truncation dropped it. Use an oracle-context answer test to separate retrieval from generation failures. Fix the observed stage and rerun a held-out slice.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The reversal policy was ingested, but its heading was removed and the chunk contains only 'this process'. Restoring title/section context may help more than a stronger generator.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Candidate recall, reranker retention, final-context coverage, answer correctness and latency by query class.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: More candidates improve recall but can increase reranker cost and distraction. Better metadata may be cheaper and more reliable than extra model calls.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would inspect the missing source through every stage, compare lexical/dense paths and run an oracle-context experiment. The fix depends on whether the source was absent, filtered, misranked or dropped; changing the LLM first would not isolate the problem.

followups.question: Why hybrid retrieval?
followups.answer: Exact procedure/API terms and semantic paraphrases provide complementary signals. Compare the union's recall before assuming fusion helps.

followups.question: What if the correct chunk is ranked 40?
followups.answer: Increasing candidate depth and reranking may help, but measure added cost. Also inspect why the first-stage rank is poor.

followups.question: What if it is never retrieved?
followups.answer: A reranker cannot recover it. Fix parsing, indexing, embedding/query alignment or filters, or search additional authorized sources.

followups.question: Would query rewriting help?
followups.answer: Only if language mismatch is the cause. Preserve product, date, negation and identifiers, and retain original-query retrieval as a baseline.

followups.question: How do you avoid overfitting the fix?
followups.answer: Test other procedure families and exact-code queries on held-out examples, not only the one failure you just inspected.

questions.title: Retrieval has high recall but low precision. Should you reduce top-k?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: The system finds needed material but also too much noise. Reducing top-k is one option, not an automatic solution.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Candidate retrieval -> relevance labels -> fusion -> reranker -> diversity/deduplication -> evidence budget -> answer evaluation.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Measure candidate recall separately from selected-context precision. Improve ranking, metadata applicability and duplicate handling before simply cutting candidates. A high candidate top-k followed by a small precise context can preserve recall. Evaluate multi-hop tasks that require several sources and unanswerable questions where all candidates may be weak.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Fifty candidates include all three required policies, but the top five are near-duplicates. Diversifying after relevance ranking can recover the other evidence without sending all 50 to generation.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Precision@k, Recall@k, nDCG, required-evidence coverage, selected-context tokens and final answer correctness.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Tight context reduces noise/cost but can omit qualifiers. Optimize the full answer, not one retrieval metric in isolation.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would preserve a high-recall candidate pool, then improve ranking and context selection. I would reduce final context only after checking evidence coverage, especially on multi-source questions.

followups.question: Why not set top-k to one?
followups.answer: A single-source task may tolerate it, but multi-hop or exception questions may require several sources. Tune for the task distribution.

followups.question: Can a score threshold solve it?
followups.answer: Scores need calibration and vary by query/model. A single unvalidated threshold may reject relevant evidence unevenly.

followups.question: What role does a reranker play?
followups.answer: It assesses query-candidate interaction more closely, within the retrieved set. Validate domain performance and latency.

followups.question: How do you measure redundancy?
followups.answer: Track repeated source/span overlap and unique required evidence retained. Diversity is useful only when relevance stays adequate.

questions.title: The model answers confidently when no source contains the answer. What changes?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Make missing evidence an explicit outcome and teach the system to clarify or abstain.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Authorized retrieval -> evidence sufficiency/coverage -> grounded generation or clarification -> claim support/citation checks -> answer or abstention -> evaluation and feedback.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Build answerable and unanswerable test sets, including tempting near-matches. Use source quality, relevance, coverage and conflict signals calibrated against labels. Require important claims to be supported and avoid treating a model's self-reported confidence as a probability. Prompt instructions help but cannot guarantee compliance. Keep deterministic checks for source IDs and sensitive operations outside the model.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A policy mentions review frequency but no guaranteed approval deadline. The answer should say the deadline is not established in the available evidence rather than infer one.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Unsupported-claim rate, false answers on unanswerable tasks, accepted-answer correctness, coverage, false abstention and citation precision.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Conservative answering reduces unsupported claims but may frustrate users. Calibrated thresholds and useful clarification can improve that balance.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would evaluate missing-evidence cases explicitly, add a calibrated sufficiency gate and verify important claims against sources. I would measure both unsafe guessing and unnecessary abstention, because a useful system needs the right balance.

followups.question: Is temperature zero enough?
followups.answer: No. The most likely continuation can still be an unsupported guess.

followups.question: Can a second LLM verify it?
followups.answer: It can help but may share the same blind spot. Calibrate against humans and include contradictions and plausible unsupported claims.

followups.question: What if the source itself is wrong?
followups.answer: Grounding can be faithful to bad evidence. Validate source authority/freshness and measure factual correctness separately.

followups.question: How do you avoid excessive refusal?
followups.answer: Tune the risk-coverage trade-off and offer targeted clarification or an appropriate source/escalation path.

followups.question: Does citing a page prove support?
followups.answer: No. Check whether the specific passage entails the claim, including units, dates and exceptions.

questions.title: Users wait 8-10 seconds for a RAG answer. How do you reduce latency?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Measure where time goes before optimizing. Queueing, retrieval, reranking and generation require different fixes.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Arrival -> queue -> query embedding/rewrite -> parallel lexical+dense search -> reranking -> context assembly -> model prefill/decode -> delivery. Trace each stage and retain failed/time-out outcomes.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Define end-to-end boundaries and separate TTFT from completion time. Inspect prompt/output lengths, provider throttling, queue age and cache mix. Parallelize independent retrieval, reuse safe connections and cache valid repeated work. Reduce reranker candidates only after checking recall. Trim irrelevant context without removing required evidence. For self-hosting inspect batching/KV pressure; for APIs inspect provider quotas and network timing. Streaming improves perceived progress but does not reduce total work or suit every output-validation requirement.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Retrieval takes 100 ms while 5 seconds are spent waiting for a model slot. Replacing the vector index will not solve the dominant delay.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: End-to-end p50/p95/p99, stage spans, queue age, TTFT/TPOT, output length, errors and cost per correct completed task.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Faster models and smaller contexts can hurt quality; more capacity costs money; caching adds invalidation work. Optimize under explicit quality and reliability constraints.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would trace the whole path, separate waiting from work and fix the dominant stage. I would compare the change under realistic load, keeping answer quality and timeouts visible rather than reporting only faster successful requests.

followups.question: Why not immediately use a smaller model?
followups.answer: It may help generation but reduce quality and leave queueing elsewhere unchanged. Measure and evaluate the end-to-end trade-off.

followups.question: Can I cache every answer?
followups.answer: Only when identity, permissions, source freshness and input semantics permit. Financial values and personalized answers need stricter controls.

followups.question: What if p50 is good but p99 is bad?
followups.answer: Inspect bursts, long prompts, slow dependencies, retries and noisy tenants. Use bounded admission and fairness rather than hiding slow cases in averages.

followups.question: How do you test the fix?
followups.answer: Replay representative workload at fixed offered load with long/short requests, failures and cold/warm cache conditions. Report quality and errors alongside speed.

followups.question: How do you set the latency budget?
followups.answer: Allocate an illustrative target across stages, then revise using measurements and dependencies. A budget is a design constraint, not a claim of achieved performance.

questions.title: You changed both chunking and embeddings. How do you prove the system improved?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Compare controlled versions on a held-out dataset and inspect which change caused which effect.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Versioned corpus and gold cases -> baseline -> chunking-only candidate -> embedding-only candidate -> combined candidate -> retrieval/answer/cost evaluation -> review -> shadow/canary -> rollout or rollback.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Freeze data snapshots, source permissions and generation configuration for a controlled comparison. Reindex correctly for each embedding/chunking configuration. Evaluate exact-code, paraphrase, table, multi-hop and unanswerable slices. Use paired query comparisons and uncertainty estimates rather than treating tiny score differences as definitive. Keep tuning separate from the final test and preserve a rollback-compatible index.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The combined system improves average recall but harms error-code queries. An ablation shows the new embedding caused the regression while chunking helped prose; this suggests a targeted fix rather than accepting the average gain blindly.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Paired win/loss, Recall@k/nDCG, supported/correct answers, false abstention, cost, latency and permission test outcomes.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Full factorial experiments cost more but clarify interactions. A smaller representative evaluation is useful initially, provided uncertainty is acknowledged.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would separate the changes through ablations, evaluate on an untouched representative set and inspect critical slices. I would then shadow or canary the complete configuration, with explicit rollback gates and measured cost-quality trade-offs.

followups.question: What is a golden dataset?
followups.answer: Curated questions with expected outcomes and evidence, versioned with a clear labeling rubric and reviewed for leakage/staleness.

followups.question: Can I use an LLM judge?
followups.answer: Yes as a calibrated instrument. Compare with human labels, randomize answer order in pairwise judging and record judge/prompt versions.

followups.question: Why not use production thumbs-up only?
followups.answer: Feedback is biased toward users who respond and may reflect style or convenience. Combine it with controlled quality checks and operational guardrails.

followups.question: What if the new index is more expensive?
followups.answer: Report quality at matched latency/cost budgets and decide whether the incremental value justifies the resource increase.

followups.question: What triggers rollback?
followups.answer: Predefined critical-slice, access, error or latency regressions, with the old compatible configuration retained during the rollout window.

questions.title: Redis becomes unavailable. Which parts of your application should continue?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: The answer depends on whether Redis is a cache, a coordinator, a queue or the only copy of state. Define failure behavior for each role.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: API -> cache with bounded fallback -> authoritative stores/services. Global limit and job coordination -> durable/fail-safe alternative or controlled rejection. Circuit breakers isolate Redis failure from unrelated read paths.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Inventory every Redis use. A cache miss can often fall back to the source with concurrency protection, but a failed global rate limiter must not unleash unlimited provider calls. Durable job/state recovery depends on actual persistence/replication guarantees. Use short dependency deadlines, circuit breakers and bounded local degradation where safe. Avoid a cache outage causing every replica to stampede the database.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Schema cache failure can use a validated local immutable snapshot, while sensitive permission checks must still query an authoritative policy service or fail closed. This is a proposed fallback, not permission to use stale ACLs.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Degraded completion rate, database amplification, provider-limit violations, state loss, recovery time and error/latency changes.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: More fallback paths add complexity and stale-state risk. Sometimes a clear temporary rejection is safer than a misleading partially correct response.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would define Redis's role per feature. Optional caches can degrade with bounded source access, but authorization and global capacity controls need conservative behavior. I would test the outage and recovery rather than assuming Redis is simply optional everywhere.

followups.question: Can I fail open for rate limiting?
followups.answer: Only under an explicit safe policy and residual capacity bound. For strict external quotas use conservative limits or controlled rejection when coordination is unavailable.

followups.question: What happens to sessions?
followups.answer: If Redis was the only session store, continuity may be lost according to its configured durability. Design that deliberately rather than assuming every Redis deployment is durable.

followups.question: Should I retry Redis rapidly?
followups.answer: No. Use bounded backoff/circuit behavior and protect downstream services from amplified load.

followups.question: How do you test recovery?
followups.answer: Inject unavailability, latency and partial network failure; verify fallback limits, state consistency and return to normal without a burst.

questions.title: A worker crashes mid-batch and a document is later deleted. How do you keep indexes consistent?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Use stable versioned identities and a durable lifecycle so retries cannot resurrect deleted data.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Source event -> document lifecycle/version ledger -> stage jobs -> idempotent artifacts -> publication check -> active pointer. Deletion tombstones invalidate indexes, summaries and caches; reconciliation verifies completion.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Store the intended document version and lifecycle state on each job. Before publishing, compare with the authoritative current state. A late retry for a deleted/superseded version must be ignored or cleaned up. Track artifacts across lexical/vector/metadata stores and process deletion idempotently. Keep retention/backup handling aligned with policy, and audit incomplete cleanup. A queue acknowledgment alone does not prove all stores agree.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Version 2 embedding completes after a delete event. The publish check sees the tombstone and refuses to activate it, then removes orphaned artifacts.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Duplicate/orphan artifacts, deletion lag, stale-version hits, job recovery rate and reconciliation backlog.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Versioning and tombstones add storage/state complexity but make asynchronous recovery explainable and auditable.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would make the lifecycle ledger authoritative and require every publish/retry to check the current version and deletion state. Stable IDs make retries safe, while tombstones and reconciliation keep multiple indexes and caches consistent.

followups.question: Why not use random chunk IDs on retry?
followups.answer: It creates duplicates and makes deletion/reconciliation harder. Derive stable identity from source/version/configuration and chunk position or content policy.

followups.question: Can a transaction span every store?
followups.answer: Usually not cheaply. Use a versioned state machine, idempotent steps and reconciliation rather than pretending a cross-service atomic transaction exists.

followups.question: What if one deletion path fails?
followups.answer: Keep the tombstone authoritative so queries exclude the item, retry cleanup and surface deletion lag. Verify no derived cache still exposes it.

followups.question: How do you change the embedding model?
followups.answer: Build a separate versioned index, re-embed compatible source data, sync updates/deletes, evaluate and cut over with rollback. Do not mix unaligned spaces.

questions.title: Your documents contain tables, charts and scanned numerical values. What changes?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Preserve structure and exact data instead of converting everything into an undifferentiated text string.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Format/quality detection -> native parser or OCR/vision -> layout/table/chart interpretation -> structured numeric store plus searchable descriptions -> source-linked retrieval -> deterministic calculation -> grounded explanation.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Keep headers, units, currencies, row identities and chart axes/scales. Use summaries for discovery and structured values for arithmetic. OCR confidence is only a signal; validate critical identifiers/numbers against the page or authoritative source. Preserve coordinates and originals so reviewers can inspect ambiguous extraction. Chart interpretation requires attention to labels, scales and uncertainty, especially when exact values are not printed.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A revenue table is labeled 'INR thousands'. Summing extracted cells as rupees is wrong by a factor of one thousand even if every digit was recognized correctly.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Field/cell accuracy, header/unit association, OCR error, numeric calculation correctness, source-link support and review workload.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Structured extraction costs more engineering but enables accurate calculations. Vision models help difficult layouts while adding uncertainty and expense.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would retain the original visual evidence, extract structure and units, and separate retrieval from calculation. Exact numerical answers should come from validated structured data with source links, with low-confidence extraction routed for review.

followups.question: Why not embed the table and ask the model to add values?
followups.answer: Retrieval may omit rows and generation may make arithmetic mistakes. Query structured data and compute deterministically when exact totals are required.

followups.question: What if OCR changes Qwen3.5 to Qwen35?
followups.answer: Flag it with domain/format checks and inspect the original crop before correction. A dictionary should not invent an unverified model version.

followups.question: Why not OCR all PDFs?
followups.answer: Native text can be more accurate and cheaper. Use quality-based routing, since OCR may introduce new errors.

followups.question: How do you cite a chart answer?
followups.answer: Link the page/figure and describe the basis and uncertainty; do not claim exact values when only an approximate visual reading is available.

questions.title: SQL is syntactically valid but the business answer is wrong. What do you investigate?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Valid syntax does not prove the right entities, joins, dates or aggregation were used.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Original request -> semantic definitions -> retrieved schema -> join/grain plan -> generated SQL -> AST/policy checks -> controlled test execution -> expected-result comparison -> repair or clarification.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Inspect required columns and tables, relationship keys/cardinality, filters, fiscal/date semantics, units and metric definitions. Use adversarial test data with duplicates, nulls, missing relations and boundary dates to expose accidental equivalence. Distinguish parser validity, schema validity, policy validity and semantic correctness. For missing private attributes, ask clarification rather than importing a column from a generic example corpus.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An order-to-items-to-payments join multiplies payment amounts. The SQL runs and references valid tables, but totals are inflated because the plan violated order-level grain.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Semantic/result correctness, join correctness, required-column/table recall, unsafe-query rejection, repair success and end-to-end timing.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Strong semantic constraints may limit flexible ad hoc questions, but reduce plausible wrong answers. Clarification is preferable to silently choosing an unsupported metric definition.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would inspect the business plan and row grain before treating valid SQL as success. I would test with counterexample data and evaluate result semantics, while keeping execution safe. Missing or ambiguous schema meaning should lead to clarification, not a confident guess.

followups.question: What if the correct table was not retrieved?
followups.answer: Improve schema metadata, lexical/semantic linking or candidate coverage first. A generation repair cannot reliably invent missing schema evidence.

followups.question: How do you prevent bad joins?
followups.answer: Use validated relationship edges and cardinality-aware plans, then test result semantics. Similar column names and shortest paths alone are insufficient.

followups.question: Why not execute every generated query to see?
followups.answer: Execution needs least privilege, timeouts, object policy and resource controls. Some syntactically valid reads can be expensive or disclose unauthorized data.

followups.question: What does the current benchmark prove?
followups.answer: Only its defined measured outcomes. Your saved report's success and validity are distinct; do not promote planner timing or validity into unmeasured live execution accuracy.

followups.question: What if confidence is high?
followups.answer: A heuristic can be overconfident. Validate/calibrate it against semantic outcomes and reject unresolved ambiguity despite a high score.

questions.title: Scenario: A deployment succeeds but users see a blank page. How do you debug it?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Separate asset loading, JavaScript execution, routing and data failures before changing application code randomly.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Browser/network evidence -> entry document -> versioned assets -> runtime errors -> route/data checks -> rollback or targeted repair

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Inspect the console and network responses, status/content types, base paths, CSP, cache versions and runtime configuration. Verify direct links as well as the landing route. Check that HTML references assets in the deployed publish directory and that stale caches do not mix versions. Reproduce the deployed artifact locally, then repair the failing layer or roll back the exact release.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A static host publishes the repository root while index.html and scripts are inside dist. The build succeeds but the wrong directory is served.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Successful page loads, JS error rate, asset failures, route success and time to recovery.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Broad cache invalidation can restore consistency but increases origin traffic; versioned assets and an uncached entry point offer a controlled release strategy.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would inspect the deployed network/runtime evidence and artifact paths, then fix the verified failure or restore the previous artifact.

followups.question: Can every missing asset use a single-page-app fallback?
followups.answer: No. Returning HTML for a missing JS file hides the error and causes parse/MIME failures. Configure fallback only as appropriate for routes.

followups.question: Why might refresh fail on a deep URL?
followups.answer: History-based routing needs suitable server fallback rules. Hash routing avoids that particular server lookup issue.

followups.question: Is a successful build proof of deployment correctness?
followups.answer: No. Artifact paths, configuration, cache and runtime behavior need release checks.

questions.title: Scenario: Users submit the same job twice after a slow response. How do you prevent duplicate work?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Give the intended operation a stable identity and make repeat submission return its existing status/result.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Client request key -> authenticated scope -> durable idempotency record -> one job -> status endpoint -> result

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Bind the key to the user/tenant and normalized request semantics, detect conflicting reuse and persist the operation state before scheduling. Use a unique constraint or atomic operation, then handle enqueue/DB consistency with an outbox or appropriate transaction pattern. Define key retention, in-progress responses and failure retry policy.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Repeated clicks on 'ingest document' reuse the same upload/job identity rather than scheduling two embedding runs.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Duplicate effects, deduplicated submissions, stuck operations, enqueue reconciliation and completion latency.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Persistent identities add storage and lifecycle complexity but protect cost and user-visible correctness.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would make job creation idempotent with a scoped durable key, not rely only on disabling the button.

followups.question: Is hashing the full prompt always enough?
followups.answer: No. Identical text can represent separate intended operations, while equivalent requests can differ in formatting. Use explicit operation identity and documented semantics.

followups.question: What if the key is reused with a different body?
followups.answer: Reject the conflict instead of returning an unrelated old result or executing a second effect silently.

followups.question: What if the database write succeeds but enqueue fails?
followups.answer: Persist an outbox/reconciliation record and retry delivery safely rather than losing or duplicating the job.

questions.title: Scenario: A retry policy turns a small failure into a full outage. What do you change?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Bound retries, slow them down and protect dependencies from amplified traffic.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Failure classification -> deadline/retry budget -> exponential backoff with jitter -> circuit/admission controls -> fallback -> recovery probe

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Retry transient failures only when operation semantics permit it. Respect Retry-After where applicable, cap attempts and total duration, and avoid retries at every layer multiplying each other. Apply bulkheads/connection budgets and a circuit-breaker policy with bounded recovery probes. Preserve idempotency for effects and cancel work the caller no longer needs when possible.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Three retries at API, SDK and worker layers can multiply downstream attempts far beyond the original request count.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Attempt amplification, dependency error/latency, queue age, open circuits, useful success and dropped/expired work.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Fewer retries expose transient failures to users; uncontrolled retries make recovery harder. Define a user-visible degraded path.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would centralize retry responsibility, enforce a total budget and recover with jittered bounded probes rather than synchronized storms.

followups.question: Should 401 and 400 errors be retried like 503?
followups.answer: Generally no. Correct credentials/validation under a deliberate bounded flow; unchanged requests usually repeat deterministic failures.

followups.question: What is a bulkhead?
followups.answer: A resource partition, such as separate bounded pools, that stops one dependency or tenant from consuming all capacity.

followups.question: Does a circuit breaker replace a timeout?
followups.answer: No. Timeouts bound individual waits; a breaker governs calls during a failing dependency period. They work together.

questions.title: Scenario: An API streams tokens but users receive duplicated or missing text. How do you fix it?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Give stream events stable sequence identities and define reconnect behavior explicitly.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Run ID -> ordered event sequence -> persisted/cursored delivery where required -> client deduplication -> terminal status

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Distinguish a transport reconnect from starting a new generation. Use event IDs/sequence numbers, deduplicate client appends and preserve final authoritative output when the contract needs recovery. Detect partial failure and mark incomplete answers. Tune proxy buffering and timeouts, and test deploy/connection interruption. Do not claim resumable generation unless the server actually supports it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A reconnect resends the last event; the client ignores its already-seen sequence number instead of appending the same phrase twice.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Duplicate/missing event rate, reconnect success, incomplete outputs, final-output consistency and TTFT.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Persistent event history costs storage; simple restart may be acceptable for read-only chat but can repeat cost and cannot repeat external effects safely.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would define event ordering and run identity, deduplicate on reconnect and distinguish a resumed delivery from a new model run.

followups.question: Does SSE automatically persist events?
followups.answer: No. Transport features do not create durable replay storage or application resume semantics by themselves.

followups.question: Why keep a terminal event?
followups.answer: Clients need to distinguish completed output from a dropped connection that merely stopped producing bytes.

followups.question: What if the server cannot resume?
followups.answer: Disclose the interrupted answer and offer a controlled restart; do not silently splice unrelated generations.

questions.title: Scenario: A cache returns another user's answer. What is the architecture failure?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Cache reuse crossed an authorization or personalization boundary.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Verified identity/scope -> authorization-aware cache key -> current policy/freshness check -> permitted result -> audit

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Stop unsafe reuse, identify exposed records and inspect key dimensions: tenant, user/resource scope, prompt/model/retrieval versions, policy version and relevant personalization. Shared caches are appropriate only when content is truly shareable under the permission model. Hashing a question alone is insufficient, including for semantically similar questions. Revalidate permission-sensitive data at required boundaries and purge affected cache entries.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Two users ask 'What is my account balance?' The text is identical; the permitted resource and answer are different.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Cross-scope hits/exposure, cache effectiveness within scope, stale-policy hits and incident containment time.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: More precise keys lower hit rate and increase storage. That cost is part of maintaining correct access boundaries.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would contain the leak, repair scope-aware keys and authorization checks, then evaluate cache correctness before re-enabling sharing.

followups.question: Does encryption fix a wrong cache key?
followups.answer: No. An application with decryption access can still serve the wrong user's plaintext.

followups.question: Can semantic caching be safe?
followups.answer: It needs strict permission/personalization partitioning and evaluated equivalence. Similar wording does not establish identical allowed answers.

followups.question: Is prompt version needed in the key?
followups.answer: Often yes when output depends on it. Define all relevant configuration and freshness dimensions explicitly.

questions.title: Scenario: A new release changes agent state schema. How do you migrate running workflows?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Version the workflow contract and preserve a compatible path for existing runs.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Graph/state version -> compatibility check -> old-run drain or explicit migration -> validated resume -> new-run release

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Store graph, state, prompt and tool versions with run provenance. Prefer backward-compatible additions, defaults and typed validation. Test old checkpoints against the new code, or keep the old worker version for draining. For incompatible migrations define a deterministic transform and rollback plan; quarantine unsupported states rather than guessing. Reconcile pending external operations before restarting or migrating.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Renaming approved to approval_status without a migration may send old checkpoints down the wrong branch. Add a versioned transform and verify permitted transitions.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Migration success, unsupported checkpoint count, duplicate effects, resume correctness and drain time.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Keeping versions side by side costs operational effort; forced restart can lose context or repeat actions.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would treat persisted agent state as a versioned production contract and test migration/resume, not just new-run unit behavior.

followups.question: Can we delete old fields immediately?
followups.answer: Only after the compatibility window and all relevant readers/runs have migrated or drained. Use an expand/contract strategy.

followups.question: What if rollback code cannot read migrated state?
followups.answer: Plan reversible or forward-compatible transitions, retain appropriate backups and constrain rollback claims to what is actually supported.

followups.question: Why include tool versions too?
followups.answer: A valid graph can still fail or create wrong effects if argument/result schemas changed underneath it.

topics.title: ML foundations
topics.description: Missing values, outliers, model selection, evaluation and production debugging
sections: ML fundamentals: choose the right problem

intro.label: Note
intro.text: Study data quality before model selection and evaluation before deployment. Numerical examples are illustrative, not resume benchmark claims.

questions.title: What is machine learning, and how do supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning differ?
questions.section: ML fundamentals: choose the right problem

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Machine learning learns patterns from examples to make predictions or decisions. The training signal determines the learning setup.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Supervised learning fits inputs to labeled targets. Unsupervised learning discovers structure without a supplied target, such as clusters. Reinforcement learning optimizes actions from rewards over interactions and must account for delayed consequences. Self-supervised learning constructs targets from the data, such as predicting the next token; it still has a defined loss.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Ticket priority prediction is supervised classification; grouping similar unlabeled tickets is clustering; learning a control policy from rewards is reinforcement learning.

followups.question: Why start with a baseline?
followups.answer: Simple rules, majority prediction or a linear model establish whether complexity adds measurable value under the same split and costs.

followups.question: Does self-supervision mean there are no targets?
followups.answer: No. Targets are constructed automatically from the data instead of manually annotating every example.

questions.title: What is classification versus regression versus clustering?
questions.section: ML fundamentals: choose the right problem

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Classification predicts a category, regression predicts a number, and clustering groups similar observations.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Classification can be binary, multiclass or multilabel. Regression estimates a continuous target. Clustering depends on representation, distance and assumptions about group shape. Cluster IDs have no inherent business meaning, and numeric regression predictions do not have classification accuracy without a separately defined tolerance or bucket rule.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Fraud/not-fraud is classification, claim amount is regression, and spending-profile segmentation is clustering.

followups.question: Can I turn regression into classification?
followups.answer: Yes, by defining buckets, but this discards information and adds arbitrary boundaries. Match the output to the decision.

followups.question: How do I evaluate unlabeled clusters?
followups.answer: Assess stability, separation and domain usefulness. A high silhouette score alone does not prove a useful business segmentation.

questions.title: What are features, labels, parameters and hyperparameters?
questions.section: ML fundamentals: choose the right problem

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Features are inputs, labels are desired outputs, parameters are learned values, and hyperparameters configure learning.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Coefficients and neural weights are fitted using training data. Tree depth, regularization and learning rate are selected using a validation procedure. Preprocessing has learned state too: means, vocabularies and feature selection must be fitted inside the training partition rather than using the entire dataset.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Past usage is a churn feature, future churn is the label, fitted coefficients are parameters, and regularization strength is a hyperparameter.

followups.question: Is a decision threshold a model weight?
followups.answer: Usually it is a separate decision policy selected on validation data using costs or capacity. Do not tune it on the final test set.

followups.question: Can a post-outcome field be a feature?
followups.answer: Only if it is actually available at prediction time. Otherwise it leaks the answer even if its column name sounds legitimate.

questions.title: How do you handle null or missing values?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Find why data is missing, then choose a treatment that preserves the field's meaning.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Profile missingness by field, time and cohort. Distinguish unknown, not applicable, sensor failure and valid zero. Compare justified row/column removal, numeric mean or median, categorical missing tokens, indicators, model-native handling or multivariate imputation. Fit all learned imputation on training folds only, apply the same transform at serving time, and monitor missingness drift.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Salary zero means no salary; null means unknown. Replacing both with zero erases that distinction. Median plus a missing indicator is a baseline to compare, not a universal answer.

followups.question: When is mean imputation a poor choice?
followups.answer: It is sensitive to extreme values and changes variance and correlations. Median is more robust for skew, but neither restores the true uncertainty.

followups.question: What if a whole column disappears in production?
followups.answer: Enforce the data contract, alert on the feed failure and use a tested fallback or reject safely. Do not silently invent a new rule during inference.

followups.question: Can missing target labels be filled like missing features?
followups.answer: Guessed targets are not ground truth. Resolve annotation or use an explicitly evaluated semi-supervised method, retaining genuine held-out labels for evaluation.

questions.title: What do MCAR, MAR and MNAR mean?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: They describe whether missingness is unrelated to the data, explained by observed data, or related to the missing value itself.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: MCAR means missing completely at random. MAR means missingness is independent of the missing value conditional on observed variables. MNAR means dependence remains on unobserved values. These are assumptions about the data-generating mechanism, not categories a histogram can reliably prove. Domain knowledge and sensitivity analysis matter.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Random logging loss may approximate MCAR. Missing salary explained by observed job group may fit MAR. High earners preferentially withholding salary is a possible MNAR process.

followups.question: Does a missing indicator solve MNAR?
followups.answer: It may help prediction, but it does not identify the missing distribution or remove selection bias. Check cohorts and sensitivity to assumptions.

followups.question: Why can dropping incomplete rows be biased?
followups.answer: The retained population may systematically exclude certain users or conditions, changing the actual task.

questions.title: How do you encode missing and unseen categories?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: A missing value and a previously unseen category are different situations and should be handled predictably.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Mode imputation can suppress rare groups. A dedicated missing token preserves absence. An unknown-category path handles new values without crashing or changing column order. questions.title: How do you identify outliers?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Look for observations that differ strongly from the expected pattern, then determine whether they are errors or meaningful rare cases.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Start with range, unit, duplicate and timestamp checks; inspect histograms, boxplots, quantiles and cohort-aware scatterplots. IQR fences use Q1-1.5*IQR and Q3+1.5*IQR. Z-scores rely on mean and standard deviation and can be misleading with heavy tails; median absolute deviation is a robust alternative. For multivariate relationships compare Isolation Forest, LOF or domain rules. Fit thresholds on training/reference data and validate flags with experts.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A payment of 50,000 can be extreme for a student account and routine for a business account. Segment before treating all large transactions as abnormal.

followups.question: Is every point outside an IQR fence wrong?
followups.answer: No. It is an investigation candidate. Valid heavy-tailed distributions naturally produce extreme observations.

followups.question: Why can univariate tests miss an outlier?
followups.answer: Height and weight can each be plausible but unusual together. Multivariate detection considers the relationship.

followups.question: Is an absolute z-score above three a universal rule?
followups.answer: No. It is a distribution-dependent heuristic. Validate false alerts, tail behavior and domain costs.

questions.title: How do you handle outliers in ML?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Correct documented errors, preserve meaningful rare events, and use robust methods for valid extreme values.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Verify mixed units, sensor faults, duplicates and labels first. Options include correcting known errors, excluding invalid records, transforming skew, capping with training-derived quantiles, robust scaling and robust losses/models. Audit every treatment and compare ordinary and tail cohorts. Never remove fraud merely because it is unusual. Apply exactly the same validated preprocessing during serving.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Fix a documented cents-versus-dollars mismatch. For valid long-tailed income compare log1p and robust loss rather than deleting high earners automatically.

followups.question: What is winsorization?
followups.answer: Replace values beyond chosen bounds with those bounds. It limits influence but destroys some tail information; learn bounds on training data and justify the trade-off.

followups.question: Should I remove target outliers?
followups.answer: Only if they are invalid under a documented rule. Removing real large claims can make the model underestimate the risk it must predict.

followups.question: What about production values beyond training bounds?
followups.answer: Monitor their prevalence and quality, distinguish corruption from a new valid regime, and use a documented fallback or retraining path.

questions.title: Anomaly versus outlier: are they the same?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: An outlier is statistically unusual; an anomaly is unexpected in a system's context. The terms overlap and are not universally separated.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: An anomaly can be a single unusual point, a contextual violation or a collective sequence of individually normal observations. An outlier can be harmless. Novelty detection generally fits a mostly clean reference population and scores new observations, whereas outlier detection may fit data already containing contamination. Neither score alone proves fraud or a security incident.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A 3 AM login is routine for a night-shift employee but unusual for another account. A coordinated series of small transfers can be anomalous without any extreme amount.

followups.question: Can an ordinary-looking value be anomalous?
followups.answer: Yes. Timing, identity, order and relationships can make it suspicious even when its magnitude is normal.

followups.question: How do you choose the alert threshold?
followups.answer: Use known incidents where available, analyst capacity, false-positive costs and time-aware validation. A contamination setting is an assumption about the cutoff, not established prevalence.

questions.title: Isolation Forest, LOF and one-class models: when do you use each?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Isolation Forest finds easily isolated points, LOF compares local density, and one-class methods learn a boundary around normal behavior.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Isolation Forest is a useful tabular baseline. LOF may detect local density deviations but depends on neighbors, scale and dimensionality. One-Class SVM requires careful scaling and can be costly on large samples. Compare incident recall, ranking stability, alert volume and deployment cost on representative time splits rather than assuming one algorithm is best.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A sparse point beside a dense cluster may have high LOF, while a legitimate separate sparse cluster should not automatically be labeled malicious.

followups.question: Can ordinary LOF automatically predict on new samples?
followups.answer: In scikit-learn, novelty mode has distinct fit/predict semantics. Configure it for new observations and follow the pinned version's documentation.

followups.question: How do you evaluate without labels?
followups.answer: Review ranked alerts with experts, test historical incidents and carefully justified simulations, then monitor prospectively. Internal anomaly scores are not ground-truth accuracy.

questions.title: Scaling, standardization, normalization and robust scaling: what changes?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Scaling prevents arbitrary units from dominating a model; different transformations solve different problems.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Standardization uses training mean and standard deviation. Min-max scaling uses the training range, but future values may fall outside that range. Robust scaling uses statistics such as median and IQR. Unit-vector normalization changes each sample's norm. Distance models and regularized linear models often need scaling; tree split decisions usually do not require it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Income in rupees and age in years can distort nearest-neighbor distance. Fit a scaler on training data and reuse it unchanged.

followups.question: Does standardization make a feature Gaussian?
followups.answer: No. It changes location and scale, not the distribution's shape.

followups.question: Why not fit scaling before splitting?
followups.answer: The transformation would learn validation/test distribution information. Fit within each training fold.

questions.title: How do train, validation, test, time and group splits differ?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Training fits a model, validation chooses settings, and a final test estimates generalization. Split structure should reflect deployment.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Random splitting is suitable only when its assumptions match the task. Group splits separate the same patient/customer/document family. Time splits train on past data and assess future periods, with gaps where labels overlap. Fit preprocessing inside training folds. Repeated tuning using the test result turns that set into validation.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Duplicate tickets from one incident in train and test inflate results. Group by incident before splitting.

followups.question: What if a future split has different class balance?
followups.answer: That may be the real challenge. Report it rather than reshuffling away the distribution shift.

followups.question: Is cross-validation always better than one split?
followups.answer: It can estimate variability but is costly and must respect grouping/time. Random folds cannot repair a mismatch with the deployed task.

questions.title: What is data leakage, and how do you detect it?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Leakage supplies information that would not be available at the time of a real prediction.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Audit feature timestamps, post-outcome columns, duplicate families, whole-dataset preprocessing and label-informed sampling. Use ablation tests, temporal evaluation and suspicious-feature review. A field created after ticket resolution is unavailable at ticket creation even if the training table includes it. Pipeline-based fold fitting prevents many preprocessing leaks.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Cancellation_date cannot fairly predict whether a customer will cancel in the future.

followups.question: Is high accuracy proof of leakage?
followups.answer: No. It is a reason to investigate. Validate feature availability and the deployment-matched split.

followups.question: Can oversampling cause leakage?
followups.answer: Yes, if performed before splitting. Synthetic observations can share source information across folds. Resample training folds only.

questions.title: What are overfitting, underfitting and the bias-variance trade-off?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Underfitting misses useful patterns; overfitting learns details that do not generalize.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Compare train/validation curves, cohort performance and repeated splits. High errors on both can indicate insufficient signal or capacity. A large gap may arise from excessive complexity, leakage or distribution mismatch. Compare regularization, simpler models, representative data and early stopping after diagnosing the cause.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A deep tree memorizes 200 tickets with perfect training results but fails on new incidents. Limiting depth and improving coverage can help.

followups.question: Does more data always help?
followups.answer: More representative correctly labeled data often helps; duplicates, corruption and biased samples may not.

followups.question: Is the textbook bias-variance curve universal?
followups.answer: No. Modern models, optimization and regularization interact more subtly. Use empirical validation rather than treating the simplified diagram as a law.

questions.title: What are L1, L2, dropout and early stopping?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: These constrain learning or choose a checkpoint before it becomes overly specialized to training data.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: L1 penalizes absolute coefficient magnitude and can yield sparsity; L2 penalizes squared magnitude and shrinks coefficients. Dropout masks activations during configured training. Early stopping selects a checkpoint using validation criteria. Strengths and stopping rules are hyperparameters, and feature scaling affects coefficient penalties.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Save the best validation checkpoint when validation loss starts rising rather than deploying the last epoch automatically.

followups.question: Is dropout normally active at inference?
followups.answer: Ordinary deterministic inference disables it. Monte Carlo dropout is an explicit uncertainty technique, not the default.

followups.question: Does L1 find the true causal features?
followups.answer: No. Correlation and sample variation affect selection. Predictive feature selection does not establish causality.

questions.title: How do logistic regression, trees, random forests and boosting differ?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Linear baselines are straightforward; trees model interactions; forests aggregate trees; boosting improves an objective sequentially.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Logistic regression is linear in log-odds for the specified features. Trees partition feature space. Compare leakage-safe task quality, calibration, explainability, missingness behavior and serving cost. Tabular boosting is often competitive, but no model wins universally.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Compare regularized logistic regression and boosted trees on structured risk features before introducing a large neural network.

followups.question: What is bagging versus boosting?
followups.answer: Bagging aggregates models trained using resampling; boosting fits learners sequentially to improve an objective. Dependencies and error behavior differ.

followups.question: Does logistic regression require probability to be linear?
followups.answer: It models log-odds as linear in the chosen features. Nonlinear feature transformations can expand that representation.

questions.title: What is gradient descent, and what does learning rate do?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Gradient descent updates parameters using the loss gradient; learning rate controls the step size.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Full-batch, stochastic and mini-batch methods use different gradient estimates. Excessive steps can diverge or oscillate; tiny steps can waste the training budget. blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If loss becomes non-finite after a learning-rate change, inspect the rate, bad batches, gradient norms and precision rather than just training longer.

followups.question: Why can cross-entropy improve while recall falls?

followups.question: Why shuffle batches?

blocks.text: Feature selection keeps original variables; PCA constructs lower-dimensional combinations of them.

questions.title: K-nearest neighbors versus K-means: why are they not the same algorithm?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: KNN predicts using nearby labeled observations; K-means groups unlabeled observations around learned centers.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: KNN is an instance-based supervised method whose prediction depends on distance, neighbor count and weighting. K-means minimizes a within-cluster squared-distance objective under its representation, using iterative assignments and center updates. Both are affected by scaling and high-dimensional geometry, but their objectives and meanings of k differ.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: KNN predicts a ticket category from similar labeled tickets. K-means groups tickets into similarity clusters whose IDs require interpretation.

followups.question: How do you select k?
followups.answer: Use supervised validation for KNN; for clustering compare stability, separation and business usefulness. Do not assume one elbow plot proves a universally correct cluster count.

followups.question: Why can KNN become expensive at serving time?
followups.answer: It compares with retained examples or a search structure. Indexing/approximation, representation and dataset size affect latency and quality.

questions.title: What is an SVM, and what does the kernel trick do?

blocks.text: Regularization and loss control the trade-off between margin and training violations. Kernel choice and parameters affect the boundary, and feature scaling matters. Compare a linear baseline and suitable alternatives under representative validation rather than assuming nonlinear kernels are always better.

blocks.label: Example

followups.question: Is SVM output automatically a calibrated probability?
followups.answer: No. Scores/margins require separate evaluated calibration when reliable probabilities are needed.

followups.question: What does a large C generally encourage?

questions.title: What is Naive Bayes, and why can its independence assumption still be useful?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Naive Bayes combines class probabilities with feature evidence under a simplifying conditional-independence assumption.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: The assumption is conditional on the class, not that features are independent in every sense. Common variants fit different input types, such as token counts or continuous features. Smoothing avoids zero-likelihood issues for unseen events under the chosen formulation. It can be an efficient text baseline even when independence is imperfect; probability calibration still needs checking.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Token counts can support a fast ticket-routing baseline, while duplicated correlated phrases may cause overconfident evidence accumulation.

followups.question: Does violating independence make all predictions useless?

followups.answer: Use the configured smoothing/vocabulary strategy and validate out-of-vocabulary behavior rather than allowing accidental zero likelihood to dominate.

blocks.text: A tree repeatedly asks feature-based questions to make child groups more useful for predicting the target.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Classification trees can choose splits using impurity reductions, including Gini impurity or entropy. Regression trees use suitable numeric objectives. blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A tree may split first on transaction amount and then on account age if those partitions reduce label impurity in the training data.

followups.question: Are feature importances always causal explanations?
followups.answer: No. They describe model behavior under a method and can be affected by correlation and split opportunities. They do not establish causal effect.

followups.question: Why does a random forest reduce variance?
followups.answer: Averaging diverse trees can reduce instability compared with one tree. Highly correlated trees reduce that benefit, so diversity matters.

questions.title: Correlation versus causation: what can a model legitimately claim?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Correlation means variables vary together; causation means changing one produces a change in another under a defined intervention.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Confounding, selection bias, reverse causality and leakage can create predictive relationships without causal effects. Prediction quality alone cannot identify an intervention's outcome. Use an appropriate experiment or defensible causal assumptions/design when making treatment or policy claims. Feature importance and SHAP-type explanations explain aspects of predictions, not causality by default.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Customers receiving more support calls may churn more because they already have problems. It does not prove that reducing support calls will reduce churn.

followups.question: Is zero correlation proof of no relationship?
followups.answer: No. Linear correlation can miss nonlinear relationships, and subgroup patterns can cancel in aggregate.

followups.question: Why can randomization help?
followups.answer: Under a well-run experiment it reduces systematic confounding between treatment assignment and pre-existing factors. Execution, attrition and outcome measurement still require care.

questions.title: What are a p-value and a confidence interval, and what should you avoid saying?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: They quantify evidence and uncertainty under a statistical procedure, not certainty about a claim.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: A p-value describes how incompatible the observed statistic or a more extreme one is with the specified null model and assumptions. It is not the probability the null is true. A frequentist confidence procedure has its stated long-run coverage under assumptions; a realized interval is not automatically a probability distribution over a fixed parameter. State the sampling unit, dependence assumptions and multiple-testing context.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Testing many prompt variants until one achieves p<0.05 can produce false discoveries. Use a preplanned comparison and a held-out evaluation.

followups.question: Is statistical significance the same as useful improvement?
followups.answer: No. A tiny effect can be significant with large samples. Report effect size, uncertainty and practical cost/quality impact.

followups.question: Can correlated examples be bootstrapped as independent rows?
followups.answer: That can understate uncertainty. Resample at an appropriate group/unit level or use a method accounting for dependence.

questions.title: What are backpropagation, activation functions and softmax?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Backpropagation computes parameter gradients; activations add nonlinear transformations; softmax converts a vector of logits into a normalized distribution.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Backpropagation applies the chain rule through the computation graph and is distinct from the optimizer that updates weights. Nonlinear activations enable richer functions than stacked linear maps alone. Softmax outputs depend on all logits and sum to one over the specified axis, but these values are not guaranteed calibrated confidence. Use numerically stable implementations.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A classifier produces logits for three classes, applies softmax for probabilities and trains using a compatible cross-entropy implementation that may accept logits directly.

followups.question: What is a vanishing gradient?
followups.answer: Gradients can become very small through parts of a network, making learning difficult. Architecture, activation, normalization and initialization affect this behavior.

followups.question: Should softmax be manually applied before every cross-entropy function?
followups.answer: Follow the library's API. Many losses expect raw logits and apply stable internal operations; applying softmax twice is wrong.

questions.title: How do you tune hyperparameters without overfitting the evaluation?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Search using training/validation data, reserve the final test, and compare quality against compute cost.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Choose a search space based on the model and budget, then compare grid, random or Bayesian methods using a deployment-matched split. Fit preprocessing inside folds and track seeds, data/model versions and failed trials. Repeated manual choices can overfit validation too, so use nested evaluation or a fresh holdout when estimating selected-model performance.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Tune tree depth and regularization on training folds, select a candidate and threshold on validation, and evaluate once on the untouched future test period.

followups.question: Why can random search outperform a huge grid under a budget?
followups.answer: It can explore more distinct values along influential dimensions when only some parameters matter. It is not universally superior.

followups.question: Should the highest metric always win?
followups.answer: Consider uncertainty, latency, memory, interpretability and business constraints. A tiny uncertain gain may not justify a much larger operating cost.

questions.title: How do you measure accuracy, and when does accuracy fail?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Classification accuracy is the fraction of correct predictions. It can hide failure on rare but important classes.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: For binary classification, accuracy=(TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN). Define the positive class, dataset, sampling unit and held-out split. Add confusion counts, precision, recall, F1 and cohort breakdowns. Balanced accuracy averages per-class recall. For regression use suitable numeric errors; for LLMs use a task rubric, execution success and groundedness instead of an undefined universal accuracy score.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With 10 frauds among 1,000 transactions, predicting every transaction as legitimate yields 99% accuracy but zero fraud recall.

followups.question: What should SQL Copilot accuracy mean?
followups.answer: Specify whether success is syntactic validity, execution correctness or semantic business correctness. Report successful cases/total cases, with the exact dataset and evaluator.

followups.question: Is F1 always better?
followups.answer: No. It ignores true negatives and expresses a particular precision/recall balance. Choose metrics according to error costs and capacity.

followups.question: How do you express uncertainty?
followups.answer: State sample sizes and confidence intervals using an appropriate sampling unit, and compare models using paired cases when possible.

questions.title: What are precision, recall, F1, specificity and a confusion matrix?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Precision asks how many alerts are correct; recall asks how many actual positives were found.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Precision=TP/(TP+FP), recall=TP/(TP+FN), specificity=TN/(TN+FP), and F1=2PR/(P+R) when defined. State zero-denominator behavior and macro/micro/weighted averaging for multiclass work. The confusion matrix preserves counts that percentages can hide.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: TP=8, FP=2, FN=12 and TN=978 gives precision 80%, recall 40%, specificity about 99.8% and F1 about 53.3%.

followups.question: Can precision and recall both improve?
followups.answer: A better representation or ranking can improve both. Changing only the threshold on a fixed model often creates a trade-off.

followups.question: Why inspect absolute alert counts?
followups.answer: Even a small false-positive rate can overload reviewers when the negative population is huge.

questions.title: ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, calibration and threshold: how do they differ?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Ranking, reliable probabilities and the final action rule are separate properties.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: ROC-AUC summarizes ranking across false-positive/true-positive trade-offs. Precision-recall analysis often reveals rare-positive performance more directly, and its baseline depends on prevalence. Calibration checks whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. Choose thresholds on validation data using costs or workload; do not optimize them on final test results.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A model can rank fraud well yet assign unreliable 0.9 probabilities. It may need calibration and a review threshold matched to analyst capacity.

followups.question: Does high AUC imply good probabilities?
followups.answer: No. Monotonic score transformations can preserve ranking while changing probability meaning.

followups.question: What changes when prevalence shifts?
followups.answer: Precision and calibration may change even with similar ranking behavior. Recheck current outcomes and workload.

questions.title: What are MAE, RMSE, R-squared and MAPE?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: They evaluate numeric predictions and emphasize different errors.

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: MAE averages absolute errors in target units. RMSE emphasizes large errors through squaring. R-squared compares squared error with a mean-prediction reference and can be negative on new data. MAPE divides by actual magnitudes, making zero/near-zero targets problematic. Inspect signed residuals and important cohorts alongside averages.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: RMSE can expose costly large-claim misses that MAE smooths over. MAPE is a poor unexamined choice for demand with frequent zeroes.

followups.question: Is negative R-squared necessarily a bug?
followups.answer: No. The evaluated model can perform worse than predicting the evaluation set's mean under that comparison.

followups.question: Can low mean error hide harm?
followups.answer: Yes. Systematic underprediction in expensive cases or one population can disappear inside an aggregate average.

questions.title: Scenario: A model is 99% accurate but misses almost every fraud. What changes?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Replace aggregate accuracy with a detection objective that respects false-alert cost and reviewer capacity.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Label audit and time split -> baseline and ranking evaluation -> cost-aware threshold -> shadow deployment -> analyst feedback

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Confirm labels and detection delays, then inspect prevalence and confusion counts. Compare class weighting or training-only resampling, useful features and candidate models. Choose a threshold on validation data for recall, precision or review capacity, then evaluate on unresampled future data. Monitor delayed truth, calibration and subgroup performance.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With capacity for 200 reviews/day, compare fraud recall and precision within that workload and estimate loss avoided. An all-negative predictor fails regardless of its 99% accuracy.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Fraud recall, precision at review capacity, PR curves, expected loss, daily false alerts and detection delay.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Higher recall may increase customer friction and analyst workload. Delayed labels and changing adversaries constrain automated tuning.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would inspect counts, define a cost- and capacity-aware target, select the policy on validation data and verify it on future cases.

followups.question: Should SMOTE be applied before splitting?
followups.answer: No. Synthetic examples can share information across folds. Resample training folds only and verify interpolation is meaningful for the features.

followups.question: What if labels are extremely sparse?
followups.answer: Use expert review, historical incidents and uncertainty-aware reporting. Do not claim reliable recall from a handful of positives.

followups.question: What if recall improves but complaints rise?
followups.answer: Measure intervention harm and introduce stepped actions or manual review instead of blocking every alert.

questions.title: Scenario: A feature becomes 70% null after release. What do you do?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Treat sudden missingness as a data incident before treating it as a training problem.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Data-contract alert -> source and lineage inspection -> tested fallback -> upstream repair -> replay -> monitored recovery

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Slice missingness by producer, time and model version. Check parsing, schema changes and units. Use a last-known-good model or tested missing-feature path if safe; otherwise abstain or route for review. Repair the feed and reprocess affected records. Evaluate the actual missingness pattern before restoring full traffic.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A renamed JSON key makes salary null. Fixing the parser is more defensible than silently replacing every salary with zero and retraining.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Source-level missingness, affected request count, fallback coverage, impacted-cohort quality and recovery time.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Abstention reduces coverage but can avoid harmful predictions. Final impact may require labels that arrive later.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would isolate the feed regression, activate a tested fallback, repair the source and verify affected cohorts before normal service resumes.

followups.question: Why not use the training median immediately?
followups.answer: It can be an approved fallback, but new missingness may differ from training. Alert and measure its impact rather than hiding the incident.

followups.question: Should the model retrain immediately?
followups.answer: First determine whether this is corruption or a valid new regime. Fix upstream corruption before learning from it.

followups.question: How do you prevent recurrence?
followups.answer: Version schemas, run producer/consumer contract checks and monitor field-level missingness and payload parity.

questions.title: Scenario: Deleting outliers improves the test score. Can you ship it?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Only if the exclusion rule matches valid deployment scope and does not hide important rare cases.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Tail audit -> error versus valid-event review -> training-only treatment -> representative evaluation -> cohort guardrails

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Investigate errors, rare valid events and disputed labels. If exclusions were selected by looking at test outcomes, that test is no longer untouched. Compare robust transforms/models without deleting valid tails, and define how extreme serving inputs are handled. Report quality and coverage on the full intended population.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Removing expensive insurance claims reduces RMSE but can destroy the model's usefulness for financial risk.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Overall and tail MAE/RMSE, signed bias, excluded population share, rejection rate and expected loss.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Robust treatment loses some tail detail; retaining corruption harms fit. Domain adjudication is necessary.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: A better filtered score is insufficient. I would justify exclusions and verify the untouched deployment population, especially costly tails.

followups.question: Can target caps use test quantiles?
followups.answer: No. That leaks evaluation information and changes the task. Define target handling using training procedures and domain requirements.

followups.question: What if tails are explicitly out of scope?
followups.answer: Enforce that scope with a fallback/rejection path and report coverage alongside conditional accuracy.

followups.question: What if labels are disputed?
followups.answer: Review them with experts, retain uncertainty and test sensitivity to plausible corrections instead of silently deleting them.

questions.title: Scenario: Offline quality is strong but production quality falls. How do you debug it?

blocks.label: Simple
blocks.text: Compare evaluation conditions with the actual inputs, decisions and labels in production.

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.text: Version inventory -> feature parity -> split and timestamp audit -> drift and cohort analysis -> shadow comparison -> rollback or targeted repair

blocks.label: Technical
blocks.text: Verify preprocessing, model, feature and threshold versions. Reproduce permissible live examples and inspect training-serving skew, leakage, delayed labels, new user groups and concept drift. Roll back a release regression; retrain when representative new labels demonstrate a changed relationship. Drift indicators do not themselves prove task-quality deterioration.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Training uses final daily balance while serving predicts at noon. The feature contains future information offline and cannot be fixed by adding API replicas.

blocks.label: Metrics
blocks.text: Labeled task quality, feature parity failures, missingness, calibration, cohort errors and serving latency.

blocks.label: Trade-offs
blocks.text: Drift indicators arrive before truth but may be inconclusive. Logging must support reproducibility while respecting privacy.

blocks.label: Say
blocks.text: I would reproduce failures and establish data/version parity before choosing between rollback, upstream repair and retraining.

followups.question: Is all drift harmful?
followups.answer: No. Inputs can shift without changing the target relationship. Connect drift alerts to observed outcomes.

followups.question: What if labels arrive a month later?
followups.answer: Use leading operational indicators, sampled expert review and shadow comparisons, then backfill mature-label quality.

followups.question: Should every drift alert trigger retraining?
followups.answer: No. Gate it on data quality, representative labels and a release evaluation so corruption is not amplified.
